text: Melanie Williams, Dr. Wally Baldwin, and Deb Adadjo, photographed here decades ago. Women who were once members of a secret Christian sect in the United States have told the BBC that they were coerced by the church into giving up their children for adoption. Hundreds of adoptions may have taken place between 1950 and 1990, according to former members. Some of the adopted children within the church have told us that they later became victims of abuse and neglect in their adoptive families. The claims follow a BBC investigation last year into allegations of decades-long child sexual abuse within the church, which is believed to have up to 100,000 members worldwide and is often referred to as The Truth or the Two by Two. The FBI has launched an investigation since then. Warning: this story contains details that some may find distressing. Four unmarried women told us that they had no other option but to give birth to their babies. Three of them feared being expelled from the church and sent to hell if they refused. One woman said that she was pressured to give birth to her baby to a married couple from the church after being raped at 17 in 1988. My fear of going to hell was so great that it forced me to decide to give the baby to this church couple, she told the BBC. Another woman said that she was not allowed to see her newborn baby before it was taken away forever. The BBC has also spoken to six people who were given up for adoption as babies between 1960 and 1980. One woman said that she was physically and emotionally abused in her first adoptive family from the church, and sexually abused in her second. Dr. Wally Baldwin here with his wife supervised the adoptions for La Verdad. Children born in the United States and adopted through the church are known as Baldwin Babies because the adoptions were overseen by Dr. Wally Baldwin, a church doctor who passed away in 2004. Some of the women stayed in his home in Oregon during their pregnancies, according to a minister who used to work with Dr. Baldwin. The exact number of Baldwin Babies is unclear. The BBC spoke with Dr. Baldwin's adopted son, Gary Baldwin, who said the original records are no longer available but believed the number to be less than 200. He said that inevitably, errors were made in his father's adoption selection system, but his intentions were good. Others we spoke to also remembered Dr. Baldwin fondly. Because The Truth does not have an official leader, the BBC instead contacted six of its current senior officials known as supervisors to make comments. We received a response. The supervisor told us that any adoption he was aware of had been carried out through legal channels and that he had heard some beautiful stories. A woman who was adopted recalled seeing hundreds of photos in an album that Dr. Baldwin kept of the children whose adoptions he had arranged in Truth. Another adopted man told us that he had personally connected with more than 100 Baldwin babies and mothers. The church, founded in Ireland by a Scottish evangelist in 1897, is based on ministers known as workers who spread teachings of the New Testament from mouth to mouth. Most of the mothers the BBC spoke to believe that the workers and Truth as an institution should assume the majority of the responsibility for the trauma caused by the adoptions. If I keep this baby, I'll go to hell, says 62-year-old Melanie Williams, who gave birth to her adopted child in January 1981. At 18 years old, Melanie became pregnant after falling deeply in love with a boy from her school. Not only were they not married, but the father was not a member of The Truth, and he refused to become one. This meant that Melanie had committed a terrible sin in the eyes of the local church workers. The workers and their family decided that she could only continue attending church gatherings if she gave her baby to another family within the sect. If I keep this baby, I'll go to hell. If I keep the baby, I won't be able to go home, Melanie remembered. She gave birth in a Catholic hospital in Oklahoma, where they discreetly placed her in a solitary room. Remember that a doctor scolded her when she started crying during labor. Her baby was taken away quickly before making a sound, and she says she didn't know if she had a girl or a boy. The new mother was left wondering if her child might be dead. When she finally found out that the baby was alive, she told a nurse that she was unsure if she should proceed with the adoption and wanted to hold her baby. Never hold your baby, was the response. Years later, Melanie managed to locate her daughter, but she did not want to meet her. Deb Adadjo, 54 years old, also had doubts about giving up her baby for adoption, but felt too much pressure at the time to reject the workers, who threatened to ban her from attending church gatherings, which in Truth meant not only being expelled from the church, but also ending up in hell. She became pregnant after being raped in 1988. Remembering her newborn, she says I can still feel her against my chest at this moment. In our last moments together, I remember simply huddling with her and telling her I loved her and that I felt it, again and again, she adds. I had to let her go, I had no options. Sherlene Eicher, 63 aÃ±os de Iowa, says she never stopped thinking about the daughter she felt her parents pressured her into giving up for adoption in 1982. She was only able to briefly hold and feed her newborn before they were separated. Sherlene would celebrate her daughter's birthday privately every year. When her birthday came, she would buy her a birthday card and make a cake a couple of times, she says. She also used to write a lot in my journal asking myself where she would be, how she would be, what she would be going through at her age. Later, in 2004, Sherlene's daughter got in touch via email and they met. They are close to this day. When we finally met, we hugged and hugged, Sherlene says. We talked on the phone for two or three hours, she is an incredible woman. As a mom, I know how they feel, and I have a lot of empathy for them. I cry when I read their stories. But for my part, I have cried all the tears I can cry, says Deb. It has been like finding my tribe, says Melanie. I am no longer alone. Our mothers were afraid to hug us, our parents were ashamed of us, and the church would only accept us if we made the final sacrifice. And all these years later, we are all going to be okay.

On the 27th of January, the Court of First Instance of Aruba delivered a verdict in the case of E.R.d.M., a gym teacher, who was suspected of violating a minor student. In its verdict, the court ruled that the evidence presented was not sufficient to convict the suspect, and thus declared him innocent of all charges. On January 10th, the court took up the case of sexual abuse of a minor. In this case, E.R.d.M., a gym teacher at a primary school, was accused of raping a 12-year-old student, who was his pupil, during the school period of 2014 to 2016, and in addition, of possessing child pornography. In its verdict, the court stated that in situations involving two individuals, without any other victims coming forward, the court must first determine if the victim's statement is consistent, and secondly, if there is evidence to support these statements. For the first two charges, the violation and sexual penetration of a minor under 12 years old, the court has stated that despite the victim's statement being detailed, it was neither precise nor consistent. The court explained that there were discrepancies in the victim's statement regarding the age of the victim at the time the alleged suspect committed the act, as well as whether the victim was in a specific class or if the location changed. What did not add up was the victim's initial indication that the teacher committed the acts when the victim was in second or third grade, or when changing clothes in the locker room. According to the suspect's statement, confirmed by the court, in those classes, the students do not change clothes. After the victim indicated that the suspect committed the act when the victim was in fourth grade, at the moment the victim was changing clothes after gym class in the locker room. The court indicated that based on the testimony of the suspect, which was also confirmed by the school, prior to 2020 there was no mention of the victim's statement regarding this. For the reasons mentioned, among others, the court found that the victim's statement was not precise or consistent. Looking at the first question, if the statement was consistent, it would not have been answered, nor would it have passed to the second question that encloses whether there was sufficient evidence to support the statement. The suspect E.R.d.M. was also accused of possession of child pornography. This accusation came after the Public Ministry (OM) in its investigation confiscated the suspect's computer, which contained a number of photos that showed minors without T-shirts, among others, some that showed intimate parts and videos with possibly sexual content. It was explained that in total, there were 17 photos and two videos with possibly sexual content. After seeing and viewing these photos and videos, the court has concluded that most of these photos are selfies where the children are shown without a T-shirt, but with their upper body exposed, and this is not considered to be explicit sexual content. In the case of videos where you can see intimate parts of a person, it has been indicated that since there is no specific date when the video was recorded, it cannot be determined if the person appearing in the video is a minor under 18 years old. For this reason, the suspect has been declared free from the accusation of possession of child pornography as well. This verdict has fallen like a great shock and surprise for the parents and family of the victim, who are in the Netherlands undergoing psychological treatment due to the trauma he developed. During the treatment of the case, the mother of the victim addressed me with tears in her eyes and a voice that conveyed her pain and sadness. The suspect had inflicted immense trauma on not only the victim, but also on the entire family with his actions. The mother stated that due to the trauma, her child, who was a bright and studious student, a calm and happy young man, had attempted to commit suicide not once, not twice, but four times. The mother continued recounting how her child, who was once a peaceful and joyful person, had become someone who was struggling to survive amidst endless anguish and interminable sadness. Due to the enormous trauma he had experienced, the victim is currently undergoing psychological treatment and is being evaluated for possible admission to a psychological facility so that he can receive the necessary help. The mother expressed an unbearable pain in watching her child struggle daily with the unimaginable trauma that had been inflicted upon him. After the sentence in this case was made public, the social community reacted and expressed its disgust. Many are questioning how it is possible that the judicial system in Aruba declares a person guilty of a serious accusation like child abuse without considering the victim's voice, a minor. The group against child abuse Ta Basta published the news on their Facebook page and received a lot of reactions. Most comments confirm the people's disgust and indignation with the sentence that was handed down. On the 27th of January, the Court of First Instance of Aruba delivered a verdict in the case of E.R.d.M., a gym teacher, who was suspected of violating a minor student. In its verdict, the court ruled that the evidence presented was not sufficient to convict the suspect, and thus declared him innocent of all charges. On January 10th, the court took up the case of sexual abuse of a minor. In this case, E.R.d.M., a gym teacher at a primary school, was accused of raping a 12-year-old student, who was his pupil, during the school period of 2014 to 2016, and in addition, of possessing child pornography. In its verdict, the court stated that in situations involving two individuals, without any other victims coming forward, the court must first determine if the victim's statement is consistent, and secondly, if there is evidence to support these statements. For the first two charges, the violation and sexual penetration of a minor under 12 years old, the court has stated that despite the victim's statement being detailed, it was neither precise nor consistent. The court explained that there were discrepancies in the victim's statement regarding the age of the victim at the time the alleged suspect committed the act, as well as whether the victim was in a specific class or if the location changed. What did not add up was the victim's initial indication that the teacher committed the acts when the victim was in second or third grade, or when changing clothes in the locker room. According to the suspect's statement, confirmed by the court, in those classes, the students do not change clothes. After the victim indicated that the suspect committed the act when the victim was in fourth grade, at the moment the victim was changing clothes after gym class in the locker room. The court indicated that based on the testimony of the suspect, which was also confirmed by the school, prior to 2020 there was no mention of the victim's statement regarding this. By El Universal 31URL1659URLUniradio Informa Baja CaliforniaURLSocietyURLUpdated on 31URLOn her first day of work at a pizzeria in Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, a 13-year-old girl, reported missing since December 7, 2024, was found by the Municipality's Gender Police. The minor had gone to the establishment in search of a job and was where she was finally rescued. Given that this Tlaxcalan region is known for cases of human trafficking for sexual exploitation, her disappearance generated a rapid mobilization of authorities in the face of the possibility that she was at risk. We were notified through the people's prosecutor's office of the bulletin that the minor was lost since December 7, and the search began in our municipality and neighboring municipalities, but we did not have a report. The information was published on social media and neighborhood groups here in the municipality to locate the minor until the location was achieved, said Guadalupe Rivera, commander of the Municipal Police's Gender Unit. After her discovery and initial statements, the police ruled out that she had been a victim of the crime of human trafficking; instead, they confirmed that the minor had run away from her home due to domestic violence. She begins to cry, I tell her not to cry, to calm down, that everything will be alright, that we will notify her relatives since she is a minor and cannot walk alone, cannot take care of herself yet. She comments that she did not want to see her relatives, Rivera noted. She explained that her job was limited to safeguarding the minor and taking her testimony, while the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Missing and Unlocated Persons (FEPDNL) will be in charge of investigating if any crime was committed against her. The girl left due to abuse from her grandmother. According to the girl's testimony, she decided to leave home on her own, as she suffered abuse at the hands of her grandmother. She commented that, of her own will, she left her home because her grandmother was mistreating her. Her grandmother told her that if she didn't like being at her house, she could leave, and that's what she did, she grabbed her belongings and left, that's what the minor said, the commander pointed out. The minor, whose identity is being kept confidential for legal reasons, is the daughter of absent parents. Her father abandoned her and her sister when they were very young, while her mother works in Campeche, so she was under the care of her grandmother, who allegedly receives her badly. More than a month away from home, the minor rented in Puebla. Since her disappearance, the girl has been more than a month away from her home. According to police reports, during that time, she lived in an apartment in the city of Puebla, where she paid rent to sustain herself. Her whereabouts were discovered when she returned to Tenancingo, a municipality in southern Tlaxcala, and sought employment at a pizzeria located in the Centro colony of that demarcation. The owners of the establishment had hired her, despite her being a minor, but upon seeing her wanted poster on social media, notified the Municipal Police to avoid any potential legal involvement. When the agents arrived to rescue her, the minor broke into tears and begged them not to return her to her family. She stated that she did not want to see her relatives because her mother and father were not in the municipality and she was under the care of her grandmother, detailed Rivera. To continue with the investigations, the girl was turned over to the personnel of the FEPDNL through the municipal DIF, where the necessary measures for her protection will be determined to ensure her well-being.

The prognosis for Dulce Atahuaman Carhuancho was grim. Doctors at Oschner Lafayette General Hospital in Louisiana told her family that the 21-year-old woman was likely not going to survive the cerebral hemorrhage she was suffering from. Her lawyers believe that it was a result of the trauma she suffered while being held at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center (SLIPC), a detention center exclusive to immigrant women, operated by the private prison company Geo Group, valued at $5 billion. A Peruvian national, Carhuancho arrived at SLIPC after being detained in Arizona, where she informed immigration authorities that she was seeking political asylum. She spent a month in the detention center before being rushed to Oschner Lafayette Hospital, where, according to a lawsuit filed against Geo, she was admitted with evidence consistent with repeated sexual abuse and trauma, including significant hematomas around her buttocks. Carhuancho survived, but suffered brain damage. He was released from the custody of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (ICE) after receiving a hospital discharge at the end of 2023. However, he still has difficulty walking without assistance, often requires assistance to use the bathroom, and only began eating on his own again in July, according to his family's lawyers, who spoke with Forbes. To this day, he does not remember what happened to him inside SLIPC. Geo Group provided little explanation. Carhuancho's family filed a lawsuit against the company, alleging multiple failures in protecting Dulce and an attempt to cover up their negligence. They claim the company did not explain how he suffered his injuries and provided almost no information about his stay in SLIPC. The company denied all accusations. Now, a year and a half after the incident, Carhuancho's family claims that the detention center still has not provided an explanation for the origin of their injuries. To our knowledge, Geo did nothing, said Jill Craft, one of the young woman's lawyers, who filed the lawsuit in September. What happened to our client is a tragedy, she commented. On the other hand, Geo's spokesperson, Christopher Ferreira, told Forbes that the company denied all accusations in the Carhuancho lawsuit, calling them unfounded. The litigation continues. As the administration of Donald Trump accelerated what promises to be the largest mass deportation effort in U.S. history, the accusations of the Carhuancho family and other victims raise serious doubts about how a system already overwhelmed will handle a unprecedented increase in the number of detainees. A review conducted by Forbes of over 20 lawsuits filed against Geo and its main competitor, CoreCivic, in the past year, along with interviews with former employees, revealed recurring allegations of poor management, staff shortages, and hazardous conditions in their facilities (all cases are still ongoing, except for one that was resolved out of court). A recent report by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) on deaths in ICE detention centers between 2017 and 2021 found that of the 52 reported immigrant deaths, 18 occurred in CoreCivic facilities and 13 in Geo centers. The report concluded that 95% of these deaths were preventable. Negligence and Human Rights ViolationsIn 2018, Geo Group also received penalties for medical care deficiencies at its Aurora Detention Center in Colorado, following the death of a detainee after he was taken off his medication for opioid use disorder, according to the ACLU report. Geo declined to comment on the report. The same report also recorded two suicides at a Georgia detention center in 2018, for which ICE fined CoreCivic for failing to meet its care obligations, including failure to comply with suicide prevention standards. CoreCivic argued that the ACLU's data did not specify which deaths in its facilities were preventable and pointed out that three deaths that occurred at the Otay Mesa Detention Center took place before the company took over health services there. CoreCivic did not respond to requests for comment on the suicides Liz Casey, a social worker from the Florence Project for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, an organization that provides free legal assistance to ICE detainees in Arizona, where CoreCivic and Geo operate private prisons, stated that the testimonies of her clients reveal a fundamental disrespect for humanity within these private prisons. The conditions of cleanliness, medical care, and practically all aspects of life in these facilities leave much to be desired, she claimed. Both companies rejected these accusations and assured that they provide clean and humane facilities, with accredited medical care for detainees. A booming business with Trump's immigration policy, Geo and CoreCivic, along with their two smaller competitors, LaSalle Corrections and Management and Training Corporation (MTC), expect to benefit from an increase in demand for immigrant detention, driven by the Trump administration's immigration policy. Following Trump's electoral victory, Geo CEO George Zoley expressed enthusiasm in a call with investors in November, stating that the president-elect's stance on immigration represented an unprecedented opportunity for the company. According to his words, the business projects a potential doubling of all our services. Data from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 2023 shows that around 90% of those detained by ICE were held in private institutions, and approximately 80% of them were housed in facilities operated by CoreCivic and Geo Group. This resulted in a lucrative business for both companies. In Trump's penultimate year in office in 2019, the companies recorded record revenues of $1.980 billion and $2.480 billion, respectively. They earned roughly the same under Biden in 2023, $1.900 billion and $2.410 billion. Both consider ICE their largest client, which accounted for 30% of CoreCivic's revenue and 43% of Geo's, according to the companies' most recent quarterly results. Now, with Trump's promise to carry out the largest mass deportation campaign in US history, it seems that the prices of CoreCivic and Geo's shares, valued at $2.5 billion, increased by 76% and 75% respectively after the president's victory in November. The companies are preparing for the massive influx of detainees Since then, the two companies have laid the groundwork to secure the ICE contracts that are likely to arise from a new wave of arrests. Both presented contract proposals in response to an ICE request to expand detention capacity. And this month, the agency signed a $20 million deal with Geo and another $6 million with CoreCivic The question is, are the companies prepared for the massive influx of detainees up to 11 million in the next few years if Trump fulfills his campaign promise. Both Geo and CoreCivic received complaints about supposed hazardous and unsanitary conditions within their facilities. In 2022, a year before Carhuancho entered SLIPC, a surprise inspection of the Geo complex by the Office of the Detention Ombudsman for Immigrants found insufficient levels of medical staff, inadequate emergency response planning, and a plague of mosquitoes, among many other problems. Geo did not respond to questions about the Ombudsman's findings. Last year, the non-profit organization Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, the ACLU, and other immigration-focused groups published a report on the conditions in nine ICE detention centers in Louisiana, including four run by the Geo Group. Based on two years of visits and interviews with over 6,000 individuals, including inmates and facility employees, the report concluded that these centers systematically violated the minimum standards of care set by ICE itself and state, federal, and international laws. Denial of Basic Human Needs Among the alleged violations, denial of basic human needs, abusive and discriminatory treatment, and medical abuse and negligence, including denying a man surgery for a hernia, repeatedly denying appointments with an oncologist to individuals with cancer, and delaying treatment for stroke, seizures, and heart attacks. Geo did not respond to questions about the report. In a wrongful termination lawsuit filed against Otay Mesa Detention Center, managed by CoreCivic, in San Diego, a healthcare worker alleged that she was fired after raising concerns about mistreatment, negligence, and inadequate provision of proper medical support. The lawsuit describes the facility as understaffed and poorly equipped to handle the needs of its 1,500 detainees, and recounts a series of alleged incidents in which their lives were put in danger. Court records show that the plaintiff is in extrajudicial negotiations with CoreCivic to reach a settlement, which previously denied all allegations in the lawsuit. CoreCivic's Public Affairs Manager, Brian Todd, stated that the company provided high-level accredited medical care, and added that everyone at Otay Mesa had access to medical services 24 hours a day. Corruption, Drugs, and Abuse within Private PrisonsAt the Cibola County Correctional Center (CCCC) in CoreCivic in New Mexico, where 220 ICE detainees are being held, the magnitude of drug trafficking even surprised FBI investigators, who highlighted the large volume of substances being trafficked there. The quantities of drugs seized were exceptionally large, given that they are located within a secure federal facility, the FBI wrote in a search warrant. Todd, from CoreCivic, said the company supported law enforcement in their attempt to eradicate drugs from within the CCCC. Staffing issues also posed a problem in this facility. In a statement regarding a recent negligence lawsuit filed by the family of a victim who died from a drug overdose, a CoreCivic guard admitted to taking naps on the job and sleeping in their car between 16-hour shifts (CoreCivic denied any wrongdoing and the lawsuit was settled out of court last year). William Ontiveros, a former unit manager at CoreCivic who also claims he was unjustly fired, told Forbes that nighttime shifts often lacked sufficient staff. They didn't have enough staff to provide 24-hour coverage, he said. If the model succeeds The FBI conducted a similar evaluation. CoreCivic struggled to maintain the safe and efficient operation of CCCC, wrote its investigators in their court documents related to drug trafficking there. Taylor Smith, a lawyer from Smith Marjanovic Law, who represented several clients who sued CoreCivic in recent years, made a more damning assessment It is the state's worst facility. Todd denied the allegations of understaffing. We work to meet or exceed our daily staffing patterns at CCCC, he said. If the model succeeds, it will be too late to help people like Carhuancho, who is still struggling with her injuries. Meanwhile, she is stuck in limbo. Her lawyers claim that they were told that ICE has no interest in requesting her deportation, despite her still not having been granted asylum. But that was before Trump took office.

A recent report by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) on deaths in ICE detention centers between 2017 and 2021 found that of the 52 reported immigrant deaths, 18 occurred in CoreCivic facilities and 13 in Geo centers. The report concluded that 95% of these deaths were preventable. Negligence and Human Rights ViolationsIn 2018, Geo Group also received penalties for medical care deficiencies at its Aurora Detention Center in Colorado, following the death of a detainee after he was taken off his medication for opioid use disorder, according to the ACLU report. Geo declined to comment on the report. The same report also recorded two suicides at a Georgia detention center in 2018, for which ICE fined CoreCivic for failing to meet its care obligations, including failure to comply with suicide prevention standards. CoreCivic argued that the ACLU's data did not specify which deaths in its facilities were preventable and pointed out that three deaths that occurred at the Otay Mesa Detention Center took place before the company took over health services there. CoreCivic did not respond to requests for comment on the suicides Liz Casey, a social worker from the Florence Project for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, an organization that provides free legal assistance to ICE detainees in Arizona, where CoreCivic and Geo operate private prisons, stated that the testimonies of her clients reveal a fundamental disrespect for humanity within these private prisons. The conditions of cleanliness, medical care, and practically all aspects of life in these facilities leave much to be desired, she claimed. Both companies rejected these accusations and assured that they provide clean and humane facilities, with accredited medical care for detainees. A booming business with Trump's immigration policy, Geo and CoreCivic, along with their two smaller competitors, LaSalle Corrections and Management and Training Corporation (MTC), expect to benefit from an increase in demand for immigrant detention, driven by the Trump administration's immigration policy. Following Trump's electoral victory, Geo CEO George Zoley expressed enthusiasm in a call with investors in November, stating that the president-elect's stance on immigration represented an unprecedented opportunity for the company. According to his words, the business projects a potential doubling of all our services. Data from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 2023 shows that around 90% of those detained by ICE were held in private institutions, and approximately 80% of them were housed in facilities operated by CoreCivic and Geo Group. This resulted in a lucrative business for both companies. In Trump's penultimate year in office in 2019, the companies recorded record revenues of $1.980 billion and $2.480 billion, respectively. They earned roughly the same under Biden in 2023, $1.900 billion and $2.410 billion. Both consider ICE their largest client, which accounted for 30% of CoreCivic's revenue and 43% of Geo's, according to the companies' most recent quarterly results. Now, with Trump's promise to carry out the largest mass deportation campaign in US history, it seems that the prices of CoreCivic and Geo's shares, valued at $2.5 billion, increased by 76% and 75% respectively after the president's victory in November. The companies are preparing for the massive influx of detainees Since then, the two companies have laid the groundwork to secure the ICE contracts that are likely to arise from a new wave of arrests. Both presented contract proposals in response to an ICE request to expand detention capacity. And this month, the agency signed a $20 million deal with Geo and another $6 million with CoreCivic The question is, are the companies prepared for the massive influx of detainees up to 11 million in the next few years if Trump fulfills his campaign promise. Both Geo and CoreCivic received complaints about supposed hazardous and unsanitary conditions within their facilities. In 2022, a year before Carhuancho entered SLIPC, a surprise inspection of the Geo complex by the Office of the Detention Ombudsman for Immigrants found insufficient levels of medical staff, inadequate emergency response planning, and a plague of mosquitoes, among many other problems. Geo did not respond to questions about the Ombudsman's findings. Last year, the non-profit organization Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, the ACLU, and other immigration-focused groups published a report on the conditions in nine ICE detention centers in Louisiana, including four run by the Geo Group. Based on two years of visits and interviews with over 6,000 individuals, including inmates and facility employees, the report concluded that these centers systematically violated the minimum standards of care set by ICE itself and state, federal, and international laws. Denial of Basic Human Needs Among the alleged violations, denial of basic human needs, abusive and discriminatory treatment, and medical abuse and negligence, including denying a man surgery for a hernia, repeatedly denying appointments with an oncologist to individuals with cancer, and delaying treatment for stroke, seizures, and heart attacks. Geo did not respond to questions about the report. In a wrongful termination lawsuit filed against Otay Mesa Detention Center, managed by CoreCivic, in San Diego, a healthcare worker alleged that she was fired after raising concerns about mistreatment, negligence, and inadequate provision of proper medical support. The lawsuit describes the facility as understaffed and poorly equipped to handle the needs of its 1,500 detainees, and recounts a series of alleged incidents in which their lives were put in danger. Court records show that the plaintiff is in extrajudicial negotiations with CoreCivic to reach a settlement, which previously denied all allegations in the lawsuit. CoreCivic's Public Affairs Manager, Brian Todd, stated that the company provided high-level accredited medical care, and added that everyone at Otay Mesa had access to medical services 24 hours a day. Corruption, Drugs, and Abuse within Private PrisonsAt the Cibola County Correctional Center (CCCC) in CoreCivic in New Mexico, where 220 ICE detainees are being held, the magnitude of drug trafficking even surprised FBI investigators, who highlighted the large volume of substances being trafficked there. The quantities of drugs seized were exceptionally large, given that they are located within a secure federal facility, the FBI wrote in a search warrant. Todd, from CoreCivic, said the company supported law enforcement in their attempt to eradicate drugs from within the CCCC. Staffing issues also posed a problem in this facility. In a statement regarding a recent negligence lawsuit filed by the family of a victim who died from a drug overdose, a CoreCivic guard admitted to taking naps on the job and sleeping in their car between 16-hour shifts (CoreCivic denied any wrongdoing and the lawsuit was settled out of court last year). William Ontiveros, a former unit manager at CoreCivic who also claims he was unjustly fired, told Forbes that nighttime shifts often lacked sufficient staff. They didn't have enough staff to provide 24-hour coverage, he said. If the model succeeds The FBI conducted a similar evaluation. CoreCivic struggled to maintain the safe and efficient operation of CCCC, wrote its investigators in their court documents related to drug trafficking there. Taylor Smith, a lawyer from Smith Marjanovic Law, who represented several clients who sued CoreCivic in recent years, made a more damning assessment It is the state's worst facility. Todd denied the allegations of understaffing. We work to meet or exceed our daily staffing patterns at CCCC, he said. If the model succeeds, it will be too late to help people like Carhuancho, who is still struggling with her injuries. Meanwhile, she is stuck in limbo. Her lawyers claim that they were told that ICE has no interest in requesting her deportation, despite her still not having been granted asylum. But that was before Trump took office.

Police Find Deported Teenager Believed to be Missing in El Alto The Special Force Against Crime (FELCC) under the functional direction of the Prosecution Office conducted an operation in the city of El Alto against Human Trafficking and Exploitation of Persons in the 12 de Octubre zone, where brothels and accommodations operate, and in those circumstances, they found a 15-year-old girl who was reported missing on January 22. In the operation, officials from the Office of the Defender of Childhood and Adolescence of the El Alto Municipality and the Division Against Human Trafficking and Exploitation of Persons of the FELCC participated. At the instruction of the State Attorney General's Office, we conducted an operation with the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Human Trafficking and Trafficking in Persons in El Alto and La Paz, which was successful as we were able to locate a minor who had been missing since January 22 of this administration in the vicinity of the brothels where the operation took place. Additionally, we found three other minors consuming alcoholic beverages in a local establishment, all of whom were turned over to the Defender's Office for the relevant actions to be taken, said La Paz Departmental Prosecutor Luis Carlos Torrez. In turn, the Anti-Human Trafficking Prosecutor of the city of El Alto, Lidia Yujra, reported that the Public Ministry will initiate an ex officio investigation against the people who allegedly took three adolescents aged 16 and 17 into a bar in the 12 de Octubre zone to consume alcoholic beverages. The case of the missing minor will also be evaluated by a psychologist from the Defender of Childhood, to ensure her safety and return her to her home. The Departmental Prosecutor warned that operations against Human Trafficking will be constant and surprise-style in the cities of La Paz and El Alto.

The ages of the victims, ranging from 16 to 20 years old and 36 to 45 years old, reveal a desolate panorama in which five of them were mothers, leaving 10 minors orphaned. The report details that in the registered cases, various methods were employed to carry out these crimes. Eight of the victims were attacked with sharp objects, two suffered mechanical asphyxiation, and five were assassinated with firearms. Of the 17 cases reported in November, six corpses were abandoned in public roads, while others presented signs of torture, sexual abuse, and mutilation. The situation is complicated by the state of the perpetrators. Of a total of 24 identified femicides, only seven have been captured, seven have escaped, and two have taken their own lives. Four of them had prior criminal records, one died in a confrontation with authorities, and in seven cases, there is no information about their whereabouts. The problem of femicide violence transcends Venezuela's borders. Utopix also documented 16 cases of frustration and seven femicides of Venezuelan women abroad, specifically in Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Chile. In the face of this reality, the organization emphasizes the urgency of making visible and giving voice to the victims of this violence, urging the Venezuelan State and society to take urgent action in the face of the increase in these crimes and the impunity that, at times, protects the perpetrators. Panamanian authorities announced on Friday the detention of ten individuals operating for the Clan del Golfo in illegal gold mines in Panama's DariÃ©n jungle, on the border with Colombia, causing severe environmental damage. Behind all this is a criminal organization that commits crimes in the border area, which is the Clan del Golfo, said Larry SolÃ­s, subdirector of the National Border Service (Senafront), to journalists. Illegal mining can generate $12 million in annual profits for this criminal group, the main Colombian narco-trafficking cartel, added SolÃ­s. In the operation, carried out on Thursday, and attended by an AFP collaborator and other local media, seven Panamanians and three Colombians were arrested. The network, in whose dismantling the Colombian army also collaborated, operated at least two mines in an illegal manner at the head of the Mangle River, 5 km from the border with Colombia. Authorities seized substances, tools, and other equipment used in the exercise of this illegal activity, said DariÃ©n prosecutor Leyda SÃ¡enz. According to SolÃ­s, the Gulf Clan uses people whom they supposedly threaten or convince to work in these illegal activities. The mines are located in areas that have been illegally deforested. text: According to the BBC, many have been victims of sexual exploitation by men claiming to provide aid on behalf of charitable organizations. Numerous Syrian women have been victims of sexual exploitation by men claiming to provide humanitarian aid on behalf of the United Nations and international charitable organizations. This was revealed by the British BBC network on Tuesday based on several complaints. The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted an analysis last year on gender-based violence in Syria and concluded that humanitarian aid was being exchanged for sexual favors in some areas of the country. According to the report titled Voices of Syria 2018, published by the BBC, there are cases of women, especially the most vulnerable such as widows or divorcees, who married officials for a short period of time in order to fulfill sexual services in exchange for food. According to the network, those workers reported that the exploitation is so widespread that some Syrian women refuse to go to food distribution centers because people would assume they are offering sex in exchange for the aid they bring home. A humanitarian employee reported that some agencies even ignored the situation because using third parties or local officials is the only way to get aid to the most dangerous areas of Syria. This exploitation was first reported three years ago and cites the account of Danielle Spencer, a humanitarian advisor who worked for a non-profit organization, who said she heard these cases from a group of Syrian women in a refugee camp in Jordan in March 2015. Apparently, local municipal men in areas like Daraa and Quneitra offered them aid in exchange for sexual relations. They were withholding the aid that had been delivered and then using these women for sex. Some had experienced it, Spencer said. Women and girls need to be protected when they are trying to receive food, soap, and basic items to live. The last thing you want is for a man, whom you trust to receive aid, to ask you for sex in return, he added. It was such a pervasive situation that women couldn't go (to receive aid) without being stigmatized. It was assumed that if you went to these distribution centers, it meant you had engaged in some form of sex work to receive the aid. In June 2015, the International Rescue Committee conducted a survey among 190 women and girls in Daraa and Quneitra and, in a report, suggested that nearly 40 percent had revealed situations of sexual violence when accessing humanitarian aid. That survey was presented at an international agencies and United Nations meeting organized by UNFPA in Jordan on July 15, 2015. As a result of that meeting, some humanitarian organizations decided to strengthen their procedures.

text: The exhibition includes 22 images that show the harsh living conditions of one of the poorest countries in the Asian continent. The Exhibition Hall of the AgÃ¼imes History Museum will host the photographic exhibition "Dibujando sonrisas" (Drawing Smiles) from Educanepal, a non-profit organization, until February 22. The 22 images included in the exhibition were captured by the founder of the entity, JosÃ© DÃ­az, during his long stays in Nepal, one of the countries in Asia with the highest poverty rate. The photographs depict the daily life of the child population in rural villages. They show a simple and humble style of life, where agriculture is the main means of subsistence. After two years of volunteering as a teacher trainer in rural areas of the country, JosÃ© DÃ­az decided to found the organization in 2002. During that period, he witnessed the devastating consequences of poverty, child trafficking, and child labor exploitation. With the help of a few people, he launched a school education project to provide education to minors affected by these harsh situations. Educanepal currently has over 2,500 children enrolled in 47 villages and has two reception houses where more than 40 abandoned girls live, many of whom were victims of sexual abuse or child trafficking. It also offers scholarships to minors without resources and vocational training workshops for girls who were forced to drop out of school. The founder now has in mind opening a secondary education student residence. A large percentage of students who complete primary school cannot continue their studies because secondary education centers are four or five hours away. This situation has the consequence that many minors end up giving up their studies, comments JosÃ© DÃ­az. In Spain, Educanepal organizes talks and workshops to raise awareness about the harsh reality of Asian countries, as well as solidarity runs, charity galas, and exhibitions such as the one hosted by the History Museum of AgÃ¼imes. The photographic exhibit can be visited freely and at no cost from Tuesday to Saturday from 0900 to 1700 hours.

Amid the birth of a global battle centered on chip development and artificial intelligence models, one of the key figures, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, was accused of committing serious crimes. This is due to the fact that the executive director and founder of the increasingly powerful company, was accused by his younger sister, Annie Altman, of sexual abuse and rape. Regarding the incidents, in the lawsuit she filed before a federal court in Missouri, Annie accused the current CEO of OpenAI of starting to physically abuse her when she was just 3 years old. In explaining that at the time Sam Altman was 12 years old, the accuser stated that the attacks she suffered not only caused her physical injuries but also post-traumatic stress disorder. In the same vein, Annie Altman accused the alleged attacks, which she claimed continued throughout her childhood and adolescence, of evolving into severe emotional disorders, anxiety, and depression. In her accusation, she narrated some details of the sexual abuse and rape she suffered, stating that when she was just 3 years old, he forced her to touch his penis and perform oral sex on him. As both grew older, the sexual abuse and rape progressed, she noted that the aggressions progressed to digital penetration of her vagina and anus, and that on some occasions Sam would forcibly perform oral sex on her. In the following years, until the early 2000s and when she reached adulthood, the sexual abuse and rape escalated, as Annie said that Sam Altman regularly penetrated her both vaginally and anally. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, responds to accusations of sexual abuse and rape After his sister filed a lawsuit against him, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, publicly responded with a message he distributed through social media. In it, the executive director of the artificial intelligence developer company disavowed the accusations, as he classified Annie Altman's allegations as completely false. Even, on behalf of his mother and brother, Sam Altman maintained that the sexual abuse and rape allegations against him were deeply hurtful accusations that have affected the entire family. In addition, the CEO of OpenAI dismissed the allegations, citing that his sister suffers from mental health issues and refuses conventional treatment, to the point of lashing out at family members who try to help her. It is worth noting that in the lawsuit, Annie Altman seeks a jury trial, as well as damages and compensation, reportedly exceeding $75,000, equivalent to over $1.5 million pesos. However, the affected party's defense has explained that the process also contemplates advancing a request for punitive damages based on the net worth of Sam Altman.

text: What is the ICE, in charge of migrant raids Photo archive Mass raids proposed by Donald Trump to detain and expel migrants began, where the main institution has been the ICE, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement. By RedacciÃ³n01 February 25, 2025 06:48 On January 31, authorities officially announced migrant raids in El Paso, where the FBI, Border Patrol (USBP), and the Anti-Drug Agency (DEA) participated, but coordinated with the ICE. The ICE, The Migra. The Immigration and Customs Enforcement of the United States (ICE, in English) is an agency of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of the United States. Known popularly as Migration or The Migra, it was born in 2003 during the presidency of George W. Bush, by fusing the old Customs Service and the Immigration and Naturalization Service. Functions It is the corporation responsible for enforcing immigration laws in the United States, as well as customs and transnational crime. It investigates, processes, and even prosecutes individuals who entered the United States illegally, especially if they are related to other crimes. Its National Security Investigations Division combats crimes such as human trafficking and trade, child pornography, and antiquities or historical piece forgery, among other types of fraud. Differences between ICE and CBP. ICE is similar to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Both are agencies under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) responsible for border security and migration, as well as the enforcement of immigration laws, but with different actions. The main difference is that the CBP focuses on border, port, and airport security tasks, operations, and expulsions, preventing illegal migrants or prohibited goods such as drugs or contraband products from entering. The ICE works more within the country with investigation tasks to detain and deport migrants, fighting also human trafficking, interior narcotics trafficking, money laundering, and interior smuggling. Donald Trump. Upon his return as President of the United States, Trump began his plan for a massive deportation of illegal migrants. He appointed a Border Czar, Tom Homan, who coordinates the ICE, CBP, and other agencies or police. The role of the ICE has been fundamental in deportation plans, as it has the task of investigating to identify and locate, especially those accused of other crimes in addition to illegal migration. Since the Trump administration, they have insisted on attacking the Aragua Train and other foreign criminal organizations that commit violent crimes, often related to narcotics trafficking and migrant trafficking. ICE Enforcement Force. According to the agency's website, it has more than 20,000 employees in 400 offices in the United States and abroad. It has a budget of $9 billion dollars, approximately 200 billion Mexican pesos, which is similar to twice the budget of the State of Chihuahua for this year 2025. It is divided into four areas: National Security Investigations Compliance and Deportation Operations The Principal Legal Advisor Office and the Office of Management and Administration.

text: SEVILLE, February 1. The Supreme Court (TS) has rejected a cassation appeal filed by an individual who attempted to challenge the ruling of the Superior Court of Justice of Andalusia (TSJA). This ruling confirms the harsh sentence of 27 years and a half of imprisonment imposed by the Seville Court for sexual crimes committed against four minors, as well as possession of child pornography. The Supreme Court's resolution, dated January 16 and released by Europa Press, reviewed the cassation appeal presented against the TSJA's ruling, which in turn confirmed the initial decision of the Third Section of the Seville Court. In the latter, it was established that, in March 2021, the defendant, S.I.B., began a series of actions aimed at gaining the trust of five minors, all 16 years old, whom he met at a bakery located in the same residential complex where the young people lived. According to the court's findings, the defendant managed to establish a bond of trust with the minors through the offer of gifts. This allowed him to invite them to his home, where he created a friendly and welcoming environment through refreshments and meals, and in which he later committed acts of sexual abuse. During these encounters, he committed touching of their genitals, as well as acts of masturbation and fellatio with four of the minors. In a particularly grave episode, one of the children agreed to be anally penetrated by the accused, who in turn was also penetrated by the minor. Additionally, it was proven that the accused offered the young people small sums of money, ranging from 20 to 70 euros, and used intimidation tactics to maintain their silence, arguing that they could get into serious trouble, which generated a climate of fear among them. The police investigation that led to the arrest of the accused revealed that in his residence, storage devices were found containing numerous videos and images featuring minors involved in sexual and pornographic activities, material that the now convicted individual possessed for his own use. As a result of these crimes, he was sentenced to an extensive 18-year prison term for three sex crimes against minors under 16, as well as an additional 9 years for a continued offense of this nature and six months for possession of child pornography, totaling 27 and a half years behind bars. The court also determined that for four years, the accused would not be allowed to approach or communicate with any of the victims, and supervised freedom was established for a similar period. Additionally, the convicted individual must compensate each of the affected minors with 5,000 euros as civil liability. Despite the defendant's attempt to appeal their sentence before the TSJA, this tribunal dismissed their appeal, which led S.I.B. to take the case to the Supreme Court through a cassation appeal. In their analysis of the appeal, the Supreme Court indicated that the same sought to question the credibility of the statements made by the minor victims, arguing that all of them had lied. However, the appellate court reaffirmed that the probatory evaluation carried out by the Audiencia had been robust and sufficient to justify the conviction. The management of the situation, according to the Supreme Court, shows that the appellant failed to demonstrate, even minimally, that the statements of the minors lacked credibility. The defendant attempted to divert attention to a specific minor, presenting them as the one who allegedly incited the others, but the Higher Court had already observed that there were no indications that the minors' testimonies were influenced by third parties with malicious intentions. The Supreme Court made it clear that it was not acceptable to assume that all the minors had conspired to invent a story about the abuse they suffered. The consistency in their testimonies, the absence of elements that would question their veracity, and the testimony of multiple victims were sufficient to consider their statements as true, emphasizing that even if one minor facilitated the initial contact, this would not exonerate the accused from their responsibility for the crimes committed. In conclusion, the Supreme Court emphasized that it is of utmost relevance that the defendant acknowledged meeting minors alone in his home under unclear circumstances, as well as the possession of child pornography. For these reasons, it dismissed his appeal.

text: Over 2.65 million Mexicans have a final deportation order. This group would be the first to be expelled, as there is already a judicial resolution that validates their deportation. Mexico City. An analysis by the College of the Northern Border (Colef) has identified six main groups of Mexican migrants at risk of deportation in the event of a possible tightening of border control by the new administration of Donald Trump, according to Reforma. According to the study, the most vulnerable group consists of unauthorized migrants with a final deportation order, totaling 2,655,524 people, of whom 50,889 have already been detained. This group would be the first to be expelled, as there is already a judicial resolution that validates their deportation. The second group consists of 2,762,290 unauthorized migrants charged with crimes, although only 62,252 are in custody. The Colef highlights that many of these charges are for minor offenses, such as traffic violations. The deportation of this group could be accelerated due to the approval of the Laken Riley Law, which orders the detention of unauthorized immigrants who commit minor crimes. A third group consists of unauthorized migrants who entered the United States in the last four years, during Joe Biden's administration, and total 619,852 people. However, the study warns that the identification and deportation of these migrants could present operational difficulties, as it would require raids and operations in spaces such as work centers, schools, and churches, with the collaboration of local authorities and approval from a judge. The fourth and largest group is that of unauthorized migrants who do not have U.S. citizen children under the age of 18 or are beneficiaries of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, with a total of 1 million 933 thousand 208 people. Following them are the 1 million 395 thousand 220 unauthorized migrants with U.S. citizen children under the age of 18 and the 436 thousand 300 DACA beneficiaries. MexicoEU Border Crisis Despite these numbers, the Colef considers it premature to predict a crisis on the northern border due to a possible massive deportation of Mexican migrants. According to their analysis, if the government of Donald Trump were to deport 2,000 migrants daily, of which around 800 would be Mexican, it would become the administration with the most deportations in the modern history of the United States. However, these 800 migrants distributed among various Mexican border towns would not generate chaos, as long as their stays were of short duration. text: Regarding the case of human trafficking involving Evo Morales, we do not want police or civilians killed. The Minister of Government, Eduardo del Castillo, reaffirmed this Friday that we will wait for the precise moment and place to execute the arrest order against Evo Morales and other leaders who have pending cases before the justice system. We do not want convulsion within the national territory, we are waiting for the precise moment and place to comply with what the Bolivian justice has determined, he stated after being consulted on the matter. Against Morales, there is an arrest order issued on January 17 by Judge Nelson Rocabado of the Fifth Instructional Penal Court of Anticorruption and Violence against Women of Tarija, within the case of human trafficking with aggravating circumstances. The determination was made in a hearing on precautionary measures in which Morales did not appear. His defense and followers of the former president claimed that the process is a political persecution to disqualify him as a candidate for the general elections. We don't want injured people, we don't want dead police officers, we don't want dead civilians, which is what Mr. (Evo) Morales is looking for, he wants to seek a convulsion, generate chaos and uncertainty within the national territory, added Del Castillo. The former president has been staying in the Cochabamba tropics since October, protected by social sectors that support and back his potential candidacy. Another of the social leaders required by the justice system is Ponciano Santos, executive of the peasants of the Evo faction, due to the events of violence and blockades in the Parotani locality, Cochabamba, from last year.

The incident occurred in the early hours of this Saturday morning on Patagonia Street at 400 Chacra II, in the city of RÃ­o Grande, where a family attacked the home of this individual after a confusing episode in public. The family of a 6-year-old discovered that the child was playing outside his grandmother's house, where a social gathering was taking place. At a certain moment, the grandmother entered, alerting that the child had been approached by a known individual from the neighborhood, who neighbors identify with a history of sexual abuse, and who appeared to be intoxicated. The woman reported that this individual, identified as Horacio Miranda, 35 years old, had hugged the child and attempted to kiss him, although she stated that she believed he was either intoxicated or under the influence of substances. A tactical police unit extracted Miranda from his residence for his physical safety, as police officers had to use non-lethal rubber bullets to disperse a crowd of about twenty people who were attempting to lynch him. Judge Dr. RaÃºl Sahade is now handling the case to clarify what happened in this confusing episode, while also ordering security measures for the accused by the outraged relatives. El Alto, February 1, 2025. The Departmental Prosecutor of La Paz, Luis Carlos Torrez, reported today that the Prosecutor's Office conducted an operation in the city of El Alto against Human Trafficking, along with the Bolivian Police and officials from the Defender of the Childhood and Adolescence of the El Alto Municipality, in brothels and accommodations in the 12 de Octubre zone, as a result of this work, a 15-year-old girl was found, who had been reported missing since January 22, 2025. At the instruction of the Attorney General's Office, we have conducted an operation with the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Human Trafficking and Trafficking in Persons in the cities of El Alto and La Paz, which was successful as we were able to locate a minor who had been missing since January 22 of the current administration in the vicinity of the brothels where the operation took place. Additionally, three other minors were found consuming alcoholic beverages in a local establishment. All of them were turned over to the Public Defender's Office for further action to be taken, said the authority. In turn, the El Alto Human Trafficking and Trafficking Prosecutor, Lidia Yujra, reported that the Public Ministry will initiate an ex officio investigation against the people who allegedly made the three adolescents, aged 16 and 17, enter a local in the 12 de Octubre zone to consume alcoholic beverages. Also, the case of the reported missing minor will be evaluated by a psychologist from the Children's Defender Office, to ensure her protection and return to her home. The operation to control human trafficking was carried out with the team of El Alto and La Paz Human Trafficking Prosecutors, FELCC police officers, and officials from the El Alto Autonomous Municipal Government's Children and Adolescence Defender Office, under the direction of the La Paz Departmental Prosecutor. The Departmental Prosecutor announced that the operations against Human Trafficking will be constant and surprise-style in the cities of La Paz and El Alto.

text: A man was arrested after being accused of raping a 21-year-old woman who was returning home from her job at an ice cream shop in the town of Merlo. The incident occurred on Route 40, just a few meters from the intersection with Presidente PerÃ³n highway, last Wednesday at dawn, when the accused was detained hours later based on the description made by the victim. The young woman reported that she got off the bus and crossed paths with the suspect, who approached her with a knife and took her to a nearby stream, where he assaulted her. According to Primer Plano Online, during the struggle to carry out the assault, the woman suffered a fracture of the tibia and fibula, while before leaving, the suspect stole her cell phone, money she was carrying, and a hat. The officers emphasized that in her statement, the victim remembered that her attacker told her "Stay quiet and walk, I'm going to rob you," as the blade of the knife ran along her neck. Later the young woman remembered that she managed to join and arrived at her home, where she asked for help from the Police, who immediately took her to a hospital to carry out the protocol of prophylaxis and provide her with containment. Once she felt able to do so, she was transported to the 6th police station in Mariano Acosta to complete her complaint, which she had already made verbally at the health center with a description of the suspect. On the other hand, prosecutor Patricio Ventricelli, from the 6th Prosecutor's Office in MorÃ³n, ordered that the case be handled with the proper protocol for cases of abuse. He then gave instructions to the personnel from the local police station and the DDI to search for the suspect, whom the victim had provided with details. Following the woman's statements, they found the man, who turned out to be a neighbor from the area where the sexual assault occurred. Finally, the authorities determined that it is Jonathan Gabriel Quiroga, who was detained under charges of severe gender-based violence, aggravated sexual abuse with double penetration, and using a weapon.

text: Following the outrageous sexual assault suffered by a disabled child in the Mama Antula II neighborhood of La Banda, Santiago del Estero, the Sexual Integrity Crimes Unit will implement a series of measures. The serious incident came to light when a woman presented herself at the police station and reported that her 13-year-old son, who has developmental delay, had been sexually assaulted by his neighbors, aged 10 to 13. In response to the mother's statements, the Sexual Integrity Crimes Unit in Banda, represented by Dr. Daniela Yslas, immediately ordered the child to be taken to the forensic doctor. There, it was reportedly confirmed by the medical report that the child had injuries consistent with sexual abuse, and the representative of the Public Prosecutor's Office immediately ordered a series of measures to be taken, including intervention by the National Anti- Trafficking and Child Protection System (Subnaf). According to sources close to the case, in the next week, through a Gessell Chamber, the psychologists' team will interview the child to obtain more information about the aberrant incident. It is worth noting that, according to the mother's complaint, the child, despite his limitations in communication, reported being attacked by at least five neighbors when he went out to play in the street. In the framework of the investigation, Dr. Yslas will also personally interview neighbors from the area who may provide data on the minors who would have perpetrated the outrage. Additionally, she requested that the Division against Human Trafficking conduct a review of the security cameras in the area that may have captured the actions of the depraved children. It is worth remembering that in a conversation with Noticiero 7, the woman said that it is something horrible that they have done to my son. The damage is so great. He is a special child. I cannot believe that he went out to play and they did this to him.

Radicalized measure to regulate abortions in minors under 15 years old. The purpose of the legislative piece submitted by Senator Joanne RodrÃ­guez Veve is to activate a protocol as soon as a minor seeks medical attention. Senator Joanne RodrÃ­guez Veve, of the Project Dignity (PD), has submitted a legislative measure to create a law that would establish a protocol for handling cases of abortions in minors under 15 years old or younger in Puerto Rico, with the intention of activating a protocol as soon as a minor seeks medical attention to undergo an abortion. It would also require one of the minor's parents, who is 18 years old or older, to provide written consent stating that they authorize the minor to undergo an abortion procedure. According to the explanatory statement, the measure aims to protect minors from abuse and in jurisdictions in the United States, it is legally required that the guardians of minors be involved in the entire process leading to a legal abortion. In this way, it is not only sought to ensure that the minor is guided, helped, and accompanied by those who have the duty to ensure their well-being, but also, with this, it is sought to prevent and combat the sexual abuse of minors, reads the measure. The bill also establishes that in 2024 the Senate's Committee on Life and Family Matters made a referral to various agencies, including the Department of Justice. The intention was to know the cases of sexual abuse of minors and the defaults with abortion clinics. Related History Women who gestate for others suffer more severe complications during pregnancy Justice presented a report where 67 cases of minors under 15 years old or less were confirmed to have undergone an abortion at abortion clinics between 2018 and 2022. Two of the 67 girls were found to be victims of sexual aggression. Meanwhile, in 32 of the 67 cases, Justice ruled out sexual aggression. In 22 cases, abortions were performed on girls aged 14 to 15 who had relationships with young men aged 18 and 19. Eight of the minors became pregnant due to having a relationship with someone more than four years older. Of the 67 cases, only 36 were accompanied by their mother or father, and in 30 cases, it is unknown whether they were accompanied or alone. If this measure becomes law, before performing an abortion on a minor, the healthcare provider must notify and obtain consent from one of the minor's parents, who must be present at the time of the procedure. The minor's identification information and the legal guardian accompanying them must be documented in the minor's file. Immediate referral to the Family Department (DF) must be made, even if one of the parents is present, and the information must be included in the file with date and time. If the minor claims that the pregnancy was caused by her parent or legal guardian, the abortion clinic or hospital must be exempt from the requirement of having the parents present during the process. If it is found that one of the parents forces the minor to undergo the abortion by force or violence, they are exposed to a prison sentence and a fine of $50,000. But if the clinic performs the procedure violating the statutes of this measure, they are exposed to a two-year prison sentence and a fine of $25,000. Former Health Secretary Carlos Mellado had already amended Regulation Number 7654 precisely to regulate the Licensing, Operation, and Maintenance of Abortion Clinics, where now these clinics are required to refer cases of minors under 15 years old or those who come to undergo an abortion under suspicion of sexual assault to the authorities. It was precisely RodrÃ­guez Veve who had requested that former Governor Pedro Pierluisi and the Health Secretary amend the regulation in March with the purpose of establishing a protocol for the management and referral of these cases. Related Health Story: Reform of Abortion Regulation for Minors Amendment to the Adoption Law The spokesperson in the Senate of Dignity also filed a bill to amend the Adoption Law of Puerto Rico to add more mechanisms to voluntary adoption and the voluntary surrender of a minor if the parents meet the age of 18 years. With this, it would be established that a young woman between the ages of 18 and 21 has the legal capacity to make the decision to make a voluntary surrender of not wanting to stay with her child. If she is given the capacity to decide to practice an abortion with the intervention of her parents, that same minor must have full legal capacity to make the determination to voluntarily surrender her baby, once it is born, the project reads. Therefore, the amendments state that there will be sufficient capacity to act and consent to an adoption agreement for biological parents who have reached 18 years of age at the time of the agreement. In the case where the biological mother or father is under 18 years of age and is not emancipated, their parents or guardians will supply the necessary legal capacity to consent and thus meet the requirements of this law.Related History The project will allow doctors to challenge a pregnant woman's will to become law. Once the law is in place, doctors will be able to voluntarily hand over a minor up to three years old to the Department of Family or an adoption agency without committing a crime of child abandonment, as long as there are no signs of abuse or maltreatment. After the law is approved, the DF will have to establish within 30 days a regulation to establish protocols once the minor is in the custody of the hospital or the DF. text: The alleged child abuse complaint at a school in Cartagena has been the subject of criticism and outrage. A teacher allegedly tied one of her students to their desk to prevent them from moving, among other alleged abuses she supposedly committed against them. This complaint was made public last Wednesday, January 29, by the student's brother who was affected by the alleged abuse case. In response to the incident, several public entities have spoken out, and an investigation was announced to determine the responsibility of those involved. The child was allegedly mistreated by their teacher. According to the complaint known on social media, the minor was a victim of aggression by their teacher. However, the events allegedly occurred in 2024 when the child was in pre-jardÃ­n and jardÃ­n at La Salle School in the city. According to the child's mother, the teacher decided to tie the child between the seat and the chair to prevent them from moving. Additionally, she reported that the woman would have attacked her on several occasions and would have shouted at her child in the middle of class. Child abuse in Cartagena Photo Supplied In response to the denunciations and the public outcry caused after the facts were disseminated, the mayor of Cartagena, Dumek Turbay, spoke out on X and assured that the secretary of education, Alberto MartÃ­nez, initiated an investigation as a result of the denunciations about the alleged child abuse in a child who studies at La Salle College. The college where the alleged incident occurred issued a statement in which it assured that they had knowledge at the same time as public opinion. The necessary measures are being taken to clarify the circumstances of time, manner, and place in which the facts developed, mentioned the educational center. In addition to this, she assured that this was done as an act of discipline to improve his emotional alteration.Note: "chichÃ­" is a colloquialism in some Latin American countries that refers to a type of bullying or harassment, often involving physical or emotional abuse. A video shared by the news channel shows a member of the school telling parents that the teacher claimed they knew about the measures she had taken. Teacher's statement Photo Social Media In several parts of the statement, the woman repeatedly stated that these actions on her part were to improve the behavior of the minor. However, she denied any aggression. In conclusion, she notified that she would ask the Ministry of Education to open an investigation against her to demonstrate her innocence. The teacher and the coordinator of the educational center were separated from their position while the authorities and the same center in Cartagena advance with the investigations. text: In an effort to promote the social and labor inclusion of women who have been victims of human trafficking, the Madrid City Council has successfully concluded a training program aimed at this vulnerable group. A total of 31 women participated in the program, which seeks not only to improve their employability, but also to offer them the opportunity to rebuild their lives away from violence and abuse. At a recent event, the delegate for Social Policies, Family, and Equality, JosÃ© FernÃ¡ndez, presented the diplomas to the participants, highlighting their effort and determination to overcome adversity. You are an example of self-overcoming and the diplomas you hold are the result of your strength in difficult times, FernÃ¡ndez emphasized. Furthermore, he stressed the importance of this program as a path to economic and personal independence for these women, urging them to look towards the future and pursue new dreams. The project, driven by multiple promotions, focuses on providing training in two key areas: commercial skills and cleaning of surfaces and furniture in retail spaces. The sessions, held in the last quarter of 2024 at Mercamadrid and Educarte, included 480 hours of training covering theoretical content, digital competencies, and active job search skills. The Madrid City Council not only offers this type of training program, but also has a comprehensive Municipal Network for Attention to Women Victims of Gender Violence. This network provides specific resources for women who have suffered abuse, sexual violence, and those who have been in contexts of sex trafficking and exploitation. A crucial component of this network is the ConcepciÃ³n Arenal Comprehensive Care Center, which offers psychological intervention, social support, and legal counseling. In addition, a mobile unit is dedicated to approaching women at risk in various areas of the city, providing information and access to specialized services. Complementing these resources, the City Council launched the Mariana Pineda Victims of Human Trafficking Emergency Center in December 2021, offering protected accommodation and comprehensive care for up to three months. To ensure continuous intervention, Casa Pandora, where women can stay for up to 12 months, and the semi-autonomous floor Malala, which focuses on forging an independent life, are also available. These efforts underscore the commitment of the Madrid City Council to the protection and reintegration of women who have been victims of human trafficking, providing not only shelter but also the necessary tools to begin a new stage in their lives.
