Trump vs. Petro and National Dignity as a Principle February 4, 2025 Shameel Thahir Silva In the second season of Lioness, a series by Taylor Sheridan, famous for Yellowstone, the character played by Morgan Freeman, who embodies the US Secretary of State, discusses with the CIA director how narcotics trafficking organizations have evolved into transnational giants. In the series, these organizations not only deal with cocaine sales, but also operate in illegal markets such as human trafficking. Compared to the terrorist groups that the US has historically fought in the Middle East, these criminal networks are presented as monsters that constantly threaten the country's southern border and have connections with the strategic enemies of the declining power Iran, Russia, and China. Sheridan es un maestro de la televisiÃ³n, capaz de construir historias sÃ³lidas desde una perspectiva marcadamente conservadora, muy afÃ­n a las ideas de quien hoy vuelve a ocupar la Casa Blanca, Donald Trump. En la misma temporada de Lioness, se refuerza la idea de que es necesario militarizar la frontera con MÃ©xico, bajo el argumento de que no se puede confiar en las autoridades mexicanas para combatir el narcotrÃ¡fico. De hecho, hacen incursiones militares en la serie sin siquiera tener en cuenta una consulta a los mexicanos. Lo llamativo es que en ningÃºn momento se plantea la posibilidad de perseguir a los narcotraficantes estadounidenses, como si todos los involucrados en este negocio fueran personas racializadas y migrantes, despojados de cualquier agencia en un tablero geopolÃ­tico donde los Ãºnicos protagonistas son los guardianes de la Ãºltima frontera que en la serie son todos militares y espÃ­as entre el mundo libre y el caos absoluto. In his first week as president, Trump launched a large-scale media and political operation with the intention of demonstrating to his bases in the United States and around the world that his commitment to the expulsion of irregular migrants is genuine. He did so under the false narrative that all deported individuals are dangerous criminals. With this large-scale strategy, trumpism makes it clear that, for his agenda, migration is illegal and not a human right. During his inauguration speech, the only mention of Latin America and the Caribbean, beyond declaring narcotics trafficking organizations as terrorists, was his emphasis that the relationship with the 33 countries on the continent would be centered on migration. That priority was clear in his exchange of statements with President Gustavo Petro on the social media platform X, where the Colombian head of state demonstrated to larger countries, such as Brazil, that it is possible to face the impositions of the US government with firmness and coherence, without coming out badly in the defense of national interests. Despite Trump's threats to drastically increase tariffs on Colombian products, and Petro's response to impose reciprocal measures on US products, this initial demonstration of strength and calculation of its consequences, not only economic, but also political, led the US government to quickly reach an agreement with Colombia. Thus, the deportation of Colombian migrants in deplorable conditions was avoided. In a recent interview with UnivisiÃ³n, the journalist insisted that this was not the first episode of diplomatic tensions with the United States and that, in his opinion, this was the worst crisis in the history of relations between the two countries. Petro responded accurately and pedagogically, recalling that the worst crisis was the separation of Panama, when the United States took that territory from Colombia. Following this episode, a media operation was launched that attempted to install the idea that Petro had given in or backed down to Trump, although the reality was different. In addition, several opinion spaces speculated about the possible consequences of Trump's tariff threat. However, a week later, the US president activated the same strategy against Mexico and Canada, arguing that they favor China, irregular migration, and drug trafficking. The response of the governments of those countries was identical to Petro's in applying reciprocal measures in response to any tariff imposed by Trump. Unlike the Colombian establishment, in Mexico and Canada their political and business sectors closed ranks around their governments in defense of national sovereignty, while in Colombia the media and certain political sectors continue to wonder if dignity is a relevant value in international relations. These episodes serve as a reminder to those nostalgic for neoliberalism that politics is not reduced to simple commercial exchanges or the pursuit of a favorable balance of payments for the country's large business leaders. Politics is also symbols, ideas, objectives, horizons of meaning, and principles. It is to push against contradictions. If we do not make politics from those values, our leaders are nothing more than simple managers of goods and people, and not leaders who push their citizens towards new horizons. The pending subject in this scenario remains a true and effective Latin American and Caribbean unity. The one we glimpsed in Mar del Plata in 2005, when the governments of the continent clearly and coherently said no to the Free Trade Area of the Americas (ALCA). The difference at that time was that the few voices that supported Bush were those of Colombian President Ãlvaro Uribe VÃ©lez and Mexican President Vicente Fox. However, although history is not linear, it has its interesting cycles, and today it is no longer the large corporations and their technocrats who govern in both countries. We need a unity that makes the Latin American life projects viable in their own lands. A unity that confronts systemic challenges such as the climate crisis and geopolitical chaos. A unit that allows us to build a horizon of sense beyond the so-called American dream that Hollywood has instilled in our common sense.

An elderly man was beaten and robbed by a woman who offered to accompany him home, but he defended himself with his cane. The accused woman has admitted to the crime and the nonagenarian has been acquitted of charges of assault and a presumed attempt at sexual abuse, which have been dismissed. A nonagenarian and two women arrived at the trial, all charged as defendants, but only one of them has been convicted. A plea agreement has imposed 22 months in prison on a woman, born in Ecuador and with no prior criminal record, who on Tuesday admitted in the viewing room of Ourense's Penal 1 that she beat and robbed an elderly man in O CarballiÃ±o on July 6, 2022, after offering to accompany him home following an invitation from the gentleman in a bar. The elderly victim, of advanced age, received kicks and punches, and the thief stole 350 euros from his wallet. Defending himself with his cane, the elderly man struck the woman and managed to have her leave the residence. The elderly man suffered as a result of the violent robbery contusions, erosions, and a rib fracture. The injuries took 40 days to heal. The other defendant charged by the Prosecution was acquitted. Her defense provided documentation to corroborate that on the day of the events, this woman was on a trip to the Canary Islands. The nonagenarian man was also exonerated. He defended himself against the violent robbery with his walking stick and was prosecuted for a crime of injuries, which the private prosecution attributed to him. In addition, this party accused him of a supposed attempted sexual abuse. This suspicion was completely dismissed after the defendant's lawyer withdrew the accusation, as one of the elements of the understanding between the parties. The Prosecution saw a legitimate defense by the mayor On the initial attribution to the elderly man of a supposed crime of injuries, the Prosecution argued that, in the case of a trial, a complete exemption would proceed, because he acted in legitimate defense. However, with the consent judgment, he is acquitted. The only convicted person has the mitigating factor of alcoholism applied to them, and also it is considered that the violence they exercised to commit the robbery was of lesser entity. They must pay a fine of 90 euros for the minor crime of injuries. The 22-month prison sentence will not be served, but they cannot commit any crime in two years so that the benefit is not revoked. All parties renounced the compensation they had initially requested, another of the terms of the agreement that settles these facts with a consent judgment.

text: Rapper and entrepreneur Sean Diddy Combs would have received medical care at a hospital before his trial on sex trafficking charges, according to The New York Post. Combs, who has been detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn since his arrest last September, was recently transported for an MRI. Sources cited by the media outlet said the transfer was made at night to avoid incidents due to the high profile of the case. The medical evaluation was authorized due to persistent knee problems stemming from his participation in the 2003 New York Marathon. After the procedure, Combs returned to his cell without being hospitalized. A spokesperson for the Office of Prisons declined to provide details on the health of the rapper, citing reasons of privacy and security, and not commenting on the condition of inmates or their medical transfers. The artist's lawyer, Marc Agnifilo, also did not issue a statement on the prisoner's movement, according to TMZ. The trial for new charges is scheduled to begin on May 5. The artist faces charges including sex crimes and organized crime, which he has repeatedly denied. The defense argues that the presented evidence, including recordings of alleged sex parties, will demonstrate that the interactions were consensual. The former music producer has been under bail on multiple occasions, including after posting a $50 million bond (approximately Â£38.4 million). In December, a judge once again rejected a request for bail, stating that the government has clearly and convincingly demonstrated that there is no reasonable guarantee for the community. Over the past few months, there have been demands for misconduct against him. In November, five anonymous individuals accused Combs of drugging and sexually assaulting them in Miami in 2001. In October, another complaint accused the rapper of assaulting a 10-year-old child in 2005. Additionally, previous reports indicated that more than 120 people have filed accusations, with 25 being minors. The media fallout from the case has been significant, especially with the release of the documentary The Making of Bad Boy on Peacock, where several people accuse Combs of abusive behavior. Singer Sara Rivers, a former member of a band from the reality show Band, claimed that the rapper threatened her. He told you I'm so angry I want to eat your flesh, he said in the production. The documentary also explores theories about the possible involvement in the murder of Notorious B.I.G. in 1997, as well as cases of domestic violence against Kim Porter, the mother of his children and ex-partner. Combs' legal team has presented criticisms of the documentary, labeling it as irresponsible journalism based on lies and conspiracies. The case continues to generate great media attention as key trial dates approach.

text: In Canal 9 Litoral, we discussed this topic with Silvina Calveyra, coordinator of the Provincial Council Against Human Trafficking, who told us the following: Today we had communication with national authorities of the Federal Council Against Human Trafficking, which we are a part of, and also with Migration authorities to be able to interpret and understand a bit the resolution, because that's what it's about. In this sense, and personally, it's not good to remove controls, especially when it comes to children, girls, and adolescents under 18 years old. However, we must also understand that many times private companies, primarily land-based at the international level, do not perform the necessary controls either. This resolution deals with a question of functionality towards the sale of tickets, towards companies, but it does not eliminate everything that has to do with the function of who must control the documentation of minors under the age of 18, which are the officials of the Directorate of Migration. In this regard, we have hotter border zones where there is greater concern, but if in this way the controls are strengthened in some way, the human resources, technological, biometric data, then this request for documentation from minors will continue to be made in order to be authorized to be transported from one place to another. Controversy over this new measure Human rights organizations have expressed their rejection of the measure, arguing that it undermines the protection of childhood and facilitates the actions of human trafficking networks. The Alameda Foundation, dedicated to fighting exploitation and enslavement, stated in a statement that the elimination of documentary controls in international transportation represents a setback in the fight against human trafficking, exposing children and adolescents to a greater risk. Internationally, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) has expressed concern over the measure and has urged the Argentine government to ensure the protection of minors.

This alarming figure reflects the magnitude of a nationwide problem that affects the physical and mental health of the minors who are victims of this type of sexual violence. In a context like Peru's, where children are increasingly exposed to vulnerable situations, it is essential to provide them with tools that promote their physical and emotional self-care to prevent child sexual abuse. Teaching them to identify, recognize, protect, and respect their own body, as well as establish healthy boundaries and detect hazardous situations, not only empowers them but also strengthens their skills to build healthy and safe relationships. A child who knows their body is a child who understands that no one can transgress their physical or emotional space, is a child prepared to ask for help in any circumstance, says the specialist, who is also an expert in child sexual education. According to Dr. Vicente, the basic self-care tips to prevent child sexual abuse are as follows: Recognize and respect the body - teaching children the correct names of their body parts is the first step for them to understand the importance of protecting it. One cannot take care of what they do not know, notes the psychologist. Establish clear boundaries - children must learn that they have the right to say no if something or someone makes them feel uncomfortable. Self-care in the digital environment - in an era where children have early access to electronic devices, it is essential to supervise and guide their use. From an early age, they must promote open and honest communication, responding to children's questions in an appropriate manner for their age and emotional development. Using tools like stories, songs, or playful activities facilitates children seeing their parents as trusted figures, strengthening their sense of security in the face of potential risks. In addition, parents should be vigilant for warning signs, such as changes in behavior or mood in the child, that may indicate something is not right. Through the creation of a trusting environment, where children feel they can ask for help without fear, the capacity for prevention against possible abuses is strengthened. Benefits of self-care in children Incorporating these basic guidelines into children's sex education from a young age has numerous benefits Reduction of risks A child educated in self-care and prevention will be able to recognize dangerous situations and will be able to ask for help in time, avoiding risky situations. Healthier relationships Children who learn about respect and consent develop relationships based on these principles, allowing them to recognize what constitutes a healthy relationship. Diddy Accused of Drugging and Assaulting a Music Aspirant in New Lawsuit Sean "Diddy" Combs is being sued by another John Doe, who alleges that the incarcerated rapper drugged and assaulted him. According to court documents obtained by Variety and TMZ, an unidentified man detailed an incident from 2015 where he supposedly was violated by the mogul. The then 23-year-old musician claimed in court documents that he was scheduled to perform at a series of nightclubs in Los Angeles, including QCs 20URL. Before his performance, Doe claims that he was told that Diddy, 55 at the time, would be present and would consider signing him to Bad Boy Records if the performance went well. However, that night, Doe supposedly attended a party after the fact and claims that while he was there, one of Diddy's associates supposedly handed him a drink and told Doe that it was from Diddy. The supposed victim claims that he soon realized he had been drugged In the lawsuit, filed by lawyer Tony Buzbee, Doe alleged that he entered and exited consciousness, but woke up with Diddy touching him. Doe also believed that the rapper had performed oral sex on him. After regaining consciousness, Doe claims that he attempted to fight Diddy, but was told that doing so would harm his chances of success in music if he didn't comply.Us Weekly has reached out to Diddy's team for comment. In a statement provided to Variety, Diddy's lawyers denied the allegations, stating: "As we have said before, Mr. Combs cannot respond to every new publicity stunt, even in response to claims that are ridiculous at first glance or demonstrably false. Mr. Combs and his legal team have full confidence in the facts and the integrity of the judicial process. In court, the truth will prevail that Mr. Combs never sexually assaulted nor trafficked anyone, man or woman, adult or minor." Diddy remains behind bars after being arrested in September 2024 and charged with sex trafficking, extortion, conspiracy, and transporting for prostitution. Diddy has maintained his innocence while awaiting his trial in May 2025. The rapper also faces over 30 civil lawsuits from alleged victims of sexual assault and misconduct. He continues to deny all allegations. Over the weekend, reports surfaced that Diddy had been transferred from his Brooklyn prison to a local hospital. According to reports, Diddy had claimed that his knee was bothering him. He received an MRI to verify an old injury, but was sent back to the Metropolitan Detention Center several hours later. A spokesperson for the Federal Bureau of Prisons refused to comment, citing privacy, security, and protection concerns. If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, contact the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673).

Media PA A three-year time limit for child sex abuse victims to claim damages will be removed in England and Wales under long-overdue government reforms, said the Ministry of Justice (MoJ). The MoJ said the laws would also be refined to encourage employers to apologise for the actions of current or former employees, so victims would be more likely to receive apologies from institutions such as schools, care facilities or hospitals. The government said it was implementing recommendations established in the 2022 independent investigation into child sexual abuse (IICSA), led by Professor Alexis Jay. It is expected that the reforms will form part of bills to be presented to Parliament in the coming year. Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood said that the changes recommended by Professor Jay were very overdue. These measures help survivors continue their path towards justice, he added. Professor Jay had called for the end of the time limit for victims to file compensation claims. Currently, civil claims for child sexual abuse must be filed within three years after the victim's 18th birthday, unless the victim can prove a fair trial that can proceed despite the passage of time. However, IICSA reported that a significant number of claims were rejected because it could take decades for survivors to feel able to discuss their sexual abuse. Kim Harrison, president of the Association of Personal Injury Lawyers, said that the three-year time limit is completely inappropriate. Now it will be the accused's burden to prove that the passage of time has created an unfair trial, rather than the victim or survivor proving that a fair trial is possible, she said. The PA Media Professor Alexis Jay presented evidence to the IICSA Home Affairs Committee in January. Last month, the government confirmed that it would present a mandatory reporting duty for those working with children as part of the crime and surveillance bill. Penal sanctions will be introduced for both concealment and failure to report, child sexual abuse. The Inside Secretary, Yvette Cooper, has also promised to make preparation an aggravating factor in abuse case sentencing and review how information and evidence about child sexual abuse are collected. The long wait for IICSA recommendations to be implemented was put in the spotlight in January after tech billionaire Elon Musk attacked the government online about preparation for children. Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer accused him and others of spreading lies and misinformation, but weeks later, the Home Office announced a national review of evidence on grooming gangs and five local inquiries backed by the government. At the time, Cooper said the government would set a Easter timetable to implement recommendations in the closing report. The row between Musk and Sir Keir focused on high-profile cases where groups of men, predominantly of Pakistani descent, were convicted of sexually abusing and raping predominantly white young girls in cities like Rotherham and Rochdale. Before leading the national investigation, Professor Jay published a report on abuse in Rotherham in 2014, which estimated that 1,400 girls had been abused in the Yorkshire town.

The National Police has detained four people in Tomelloso (Ciudad Real) for the crimes of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization, and has released seven foreign women in an irregular situation who were being sexually exploited. The victims were forced to engage in prostitution in a brothel run by a woman of foreign nationality, who, taking advantage of the vulnerability of the women due to their irregular situation, forced them to engage in prostitution under threats and coercion, reported the National Police in a press release on Wednesday. The woman, who kept the majority of the money obtained from the sexual services she forced them to perform, had installed an ATM inside the residence so that clients could withdraw money to pay for the sexual services without having to leave the brothel. During the entry and registration of the premises, the agents found over 8,000 euros in cash, two mobile phones, and diverse documentation related to the investigation, as well as 10 grams of cocaine and 22 grams of marijuana intended for the clients' consumption. After the arrest of the main suspect, the National Police confirmed that both she and several family members were carrying out activities aimed at laundering the money obtained from the illicit activity of prostitution. In this sense, they sent more than 50,000 euros in several remittances to their country of origin in a few years, created two hospitality companies, and acquired several homes, one of which was donated to the arrested woman's child to conceal ownership. The four detainees have been charged with the crimes of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization. The Diocesan Delegation against Trafficking will celebrate the 7th Joint Day Against Trafficking on February 6th. The event will be co-hosted with Villa Teresita and the University of Navarra and will take place from 12:00 to 13:30 hours in the Aula Siemens of the Instituto Cultura y Sociedad of the UN. During the event, which will be presided over by Archbishop Mons. Florencio RosellÃ³, we will attempt to respond to the challenge of becoming ambassadors of hope while reflecting on the impact of trafficking on our society. Those interested in registering for the event can do so through the link. In addition to this event, the delegation will hold a Prayer Vigil at 19:00 hours in the main chapel of the Conciliar Seminary of Pamplona, where the music of the Betel group will be featured. The Vigil will serve to pray and denounce the grave violation of human rights that reduces the human being to a state of servitude and slavery. Certain acts that are part of the celebration of Saint Josephine Bakhita, which will take place on February 8th. Saint Josephine Bakhita was a nun from Sudan who was kidnapped by slave traders when she was just a child and ironically nicknamed Bakhita, which means "lucky" or "fortunate". Just like her, her sister was also kidnapped and uprooted from her family. She was forced to leave her homeland, lost her name, and was subjected to slavery and torture. Despite losing everything and being sold to different masters who mistreated her for years, Bakhita preserved her innocence and a pure heart. She did not allow suffering to take over her existence, instead transforming it into hope and never doubted the presence of God, a faith that preserved her from sadness and gave her the courage to keep moving forward. Once freed from the chains, she found Jesus Christ and his Church, receiving the sacraments to finally consecrate herself to the Lord in the Congregation of the Canossian Daughters of Charity. This year, the pilgrimage carries the motto Ambassadors of Hope Together Against Human Trafficking. A motto that fits within this Jubilee Year and invites us to bring hope to all those people who live in a world of slavery, deception, and abuse. Together, as a committed, united, fraternal, and synodal Church, on the march towards the challenge of eradicating human trafficking, so that no one else is subjected to the yoke of slavery and exploitation, in favor of a humanity of free and equal people. The Jubilee of Hope Welcome Center offers us the opportunity to embark on a path of heart transformation, which manifests in concrete commitments and actions that contribute to making possible the reception, healing, and liberation of those who need it, and, together, contributing to the transformation and construction of the Kingdom, a habitable world from the Gospel of Jesus Christ. For this reason, from our Diocese of Pamplona and Tudela, we want to promote a concrete project, which materializes in a welcome and accompaniment center for people victims of human trafficking. This project, called Navarra Against Human Trafficking, will take on the challenge of receiving, accompanying, and integrating those people, migrants, and women above all, who are unprotected. The Statistics of Human Trafficking The Delegate for Human Trafficking in the Vicarate of Social Pastoral and Human Promotion, Katya Palafox, explains that in cases of human trafficking, there is coercion and abuse of power, as well as exploitation According to the Ministry of the Interior, there are more than 7,000 people in our country at risk of being exploited sexually. The victims of human trafficking mainly come from Latin America, with Colombia and Venezuela leading the way, although there are also African, Romanian, and Spanish victims. In the Community of Navarra, the latest report from 2021 mentions 148 women who are victims of human trafficking. In light of this reality, Katya Palafox has emphasized that from the Human Trafficking delegation, they will be pushing forward a shelter and support floor for women and their children, to contribute to their labor and social reintegration. And also, the launch of a campaign to raise awareness about this reality.

text: The Civil Guard of Seville has released 52 people who were being laboriously exploited and has detained four suspected members of a criminal network in an operation framed within the Plan to Combat Human Trafficking. This group operated for several years in the town of Brenes and extended its criminal activity throughout the province of Seville. The investigation was carried out by the Women-Minors Team of the Civil Guard (Emume) of the Judicial Police of the Command of Seville, according to a press release. The perpetrators lured the victims through job advertisements published on Romanian social media, offering false job opportunities in Spain. Once they contacted them by phone, they promised legal working conditions, competitive salaries, free accommodation, and transportation. However, upon arriving in Spain, the victims were taken to homes located in Brenes and nearby towns, where they lived in extremely unsanitary conditions. In addition, they were imposed an abusive debt as a charge for transportation costs, despite the fact that this had been offered as free. To control the victims, the now arrested individuals would take away their passports, restrict their movements, and force them to work endless shifts in the collection of field crops, receiving salaries far below those established by Spanish labor agreements, with some cases experiencing threats and physical aggression. Moreover, the workers were not registered in the Social Security system.

Did you know that Mali is one of the countries where female genital mutilation is most practiced? Did you know that there is no law that prohibits and protects the lives of girls and women there? Did you know that a woman who is not mutilated is difficult to marry and is therefore rejected by her family and her community? February 6th is commemorated as International Zero Tolerance Day for Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). Currently, more than 230 million women and girls worldwide have suffered this harmful cultural practice that violates their human rights and puts their health and sexual and reproductive rights at great risk. Additionally, it is estimated that by 2030, there will be 68 million more. In Mali, where there is no specific legislation that prohibits female genital mutilation, the social and cultural context greatly hinders its eradication. In this country located in the heart of West Africa with 22.5 million inhabitants, nearly eight million girls and women have suffered this procedure. In Spain, on the other hand, around 70,000 women live from countries where FGM is practiced, of whom more than 18,000 are under 14 years old, according to the National Network Free from FGM. Alongside Red Aminata, IAMANEH, and ASICJigiya Blon, social entities and associations formed by survivors of female genital mutilation, from Farmamundi, we focus our work on promoting the sexual and reproductive rights of women and defending the right to a life free of violence for women and girls. We tell you how we work in Spain and Mali for the eradication of this very harmful practice. Women human rights defenders in Mali fight for the eradication of female genital mutilation at the risk of their own lives. Despite the risk of social stigma and their own lives, Mariam Keita, Mamadou Fadiala Sisoko, Mariam Sanogo, and Siaka TraorÃ© work every day to ensure that girls and women in their country have the right to their emotional and sexual health. With our project Itacasira, these defenders visited the Valencian Community in November to raise awareness among the Valencian society about this reality. Women need to value themselves more. We need to know more about our bodies, how they function, and how female genital mutilation affects us. Women need to know that it's negative for us to prevent any girl from suffering, says Mariam Keita, a family doctor, who during her medical studies at the university, understood that the difficulties her friends and sisters faced in their sexual relationships, childbirth, and postpartum were a direct consequence of having suffered mutilation. She currently works at a private medical clinic in Kita, where she accompanies women and girls to face the multiple forms of violence, including FGM, forced marriages, and physical and psychological abuse. Siaka TraorÃ© is a co-founder of the Sini Sanuman association, which has been working in the country since 2002 to eradicate FGM. His grandmother and mother were cutters, and he grew up seeing this practice as a craft passed down from generation to generation. Since I was very young, I have been witnessing the complications related to the practice and I have committed to doing everything possible to make female genital mutilation a thing of the past for Malian girls and women. My fight focuses on achieving a law that prohibits this practice, but it is very difficult because we are facing great powers such as the religious leaders. Despite this, we have managed to get 16 villages and more than 100 cutters to stop practicing female genital mutilation. My message is for men, because they need to know that women deserve respect. If women are well and healthy, that will have a positive impact on the lives of men as well. We must stop female genital mutilation, that is the message that Mamamodou Fadiala Sissoko wants to convey. Her activism started when she witnessed constant situations of violence against women in her family. It was then that she understood that mutilation is also a form of exercising violence over them. Today, she sensitizes women from many communities so that they can share and understand all the health complications that come from mutilation and prevent them from mutilating their daughters. Mariam Sanogo had to drop out of law school after getting pregnant out of wedlock, which provoked the discrimination and rejection of her community. This difficult context pushed her to form, three years ago, a group of women with the goal of empowering them and working to prevent their daughters from dropping out of school and being forced to marry, as well as facing other forms of gender violence, including FGM. We need more people to fight together against this practice. Alone, it's very difficult, Mariam points out. In Mali, we have formed a medical team and sensitized communities and their leaders about female genital mutilation. 89% of women between 15 and 49 years old from all over the country have been subjected to this practice. In the areas where we work together with our local partners, IAMANEH and ASICJigiya Blon, in the Kita region and the Bamako district, where its incidence is 95% and 74% respectively, we have implemented radio campaigns and sensitization campaigns to prevent this practice. Through our project, we report that mutilation constitutes a violation of the human rights of women and girls and that it is not part of any religious precept. We also warn about the dangers that this practice poses for their lives and health throughout their lives and work with traditional leaders and religious leaders to achieve their commitment to eradicating this practice, as they are the people of reference for the guidance of family decisions. It is also important the training we provide to healthcare personnel with the aim of involving the health sector in its eradication, comments Carolina Raboso, coordinator of Farmamundi's projects in West Africa. The problems it causes in the sexual and reproductive health of women are exacerbated by the lack of specialized attention, the high number of pregnancies, etc. The circumstances in which it is performed can even lead to hemorrhages and infections that are even a cause of death. The physical and psychological repercussions become chronic over the years and affect the daily lives of women. They practiced female genital mutilation on me when I was 8 years old. They told me it was a necessary tradition to turn me into a respected woman, but I didn't understand what was happening. That day remains etched in my memory with intense physical and emotional pain, accompanied by humiliation and fear. Over time, the consequences appeared: infections, menstrual pain, difficulties during childbirth, and a obstetric fistula that left me with incontinence, a survivor of female genital mutilation who we are assisting in Mali comments. Thanks to the support of our local partner IAMANEH Mali, she learned to overcome this experience. Today, she is one of the women who raises awareness about the dangers of female genital mutilation, fights for its eradication, and dreams of a future in which no girl will suffer this practice. In Spain, we accompany survivors of female genital mutilation. From Farmamundi, we have been working for years in the Valencian Community alongside Red Aminata, the only Valencian association dedicated to preventing female genital mutilation and accompanying survivors so they can enjoy their right to affective and sexual health again. The women come from countries like Guinea Conakry, Mauritania, Nigeria, or Mali. In 2024, 118 women have been attended to in social action projects, 36 of whom have passed through the Reference Unit for Reconstruction Surgery due to female genital mutilation, and 6 of them have been intervened as part of the initiative we carry out together with Red Aminata in collaboration with the Reference Unit for Reconstructive Surgery at the Doctor Peset University Hospital in Valencia. We accompany the women every time they have to go to a consultation, the process of clitoris reconstruction is explained to them, the information is translated for them, and they are told how the operation will be, the compliance with medical treatments and the nursing care they need. We are the bridge between the medical staff and the patients, so that they feel understood and accompanied in a process that is not easy. This accompaniment and follow-up are fundamental for the good medical and psychological recovery of these women, comments Aminata Soucko, Education and Social Transformation Action Technician at Farmamundi. We have also carried out an educational and social mobilization project, through which more than 40 female survivors and over 24 men from countries where FGM is practiced have passed, to whom we have offered a space to reflect on the right to affective and sexual health, transforming their ideas about the practice of mutilation. Now, it is they who are mobilizing to raise awareness and inform other women, men, and their communities, as well as student groups and society in general. Currently, we accompany 90 women and offer them comprehensive and coordinated attention, with a multidisciplinary team that includes legal advice, psychological support, and educational and labor guidance, with the aim of supporting their process of overcoming the situations of vulnerability they live and facilitating their sociolaboral insertion, comments Marcela HincapiÃ©, Social Action and Education Technician at Farmamundi. Legal advice and psychological support play a fundamental role in the integral recovery of female survivors of female genital mutilation. text: The Civil Guard has rescued 52 people who were being exploited in agricultural work by a group operating from Brenes (Sevilla) and that lured the victims through job advertisements published on social media in Romania, offering false job opportunities in Spain. Four people have been detained who were part of the group dedicated to human trafficking for labor exploitation that operated for several years in the Sevillian locality of Brenes and extended its illicit activity throughout the province of Seville, according to a statement from the Civil Guard. According to the investigation, carried out by the Women and Minors Unit of the Civil Guard (EMUME) of the Judicial Police Command of Seville, the authors lured the victims through job postings published on social media in Romania, offering false job opportunities in Spain. Once they contacted them by phone, they promised legal working conditions, competitive salaries, free accommodation, and transportation. However, upon arriving in Spain, the victims were taken to homes located in Brenes and nearby towns, where they lived in extreme unsanitary conditions, and were also imposed an abusive debt for transportation costs, despite it having been offered as free. To control the victims, the traffickers took away their passports, restricted their movements, and forced them to work endless shifts in agricultural tasks, such as field fruit harvesting, receiving salaries much lower than those established by Spanish labor conventions, suffering in some cases threats and physical aggression. Additionally, the workers were not registered with the Social Security system, according to information from the Guardia Civil.

The Valencian Community's Department of Health has updated the Protocol for Medical Attention in the Face of Female Genital Mutilation, which was first published in 2016, to achieve greater speed in detecting cases, facilitate consultation of all procedures to be followed, and protect the almost 1,300 minors living in our territory who are at risk of being mutilated by their country of origin. Among the main innovations of this update, which will be available shortly for all professionals, stands out the creation of an alert in the Ambulatory Information System (SIA) to facilitate the monitoring of cases of girls whose mothers have been mutilated. In addition, the gynecology services of any health department will be able to refer women diagnosed through a consultation sheet to the Reference Unit for Genital Mutilation Female Reconstruction Surgery of the Valencian Community, located at the Doctor Peset University Hospital. Of the women who have visited the Reference Unit for Genital Mutilation Female Reconstruction Surgery, 36.5% suffered some type of violence in their country of origin. Precisely, this reference unit evaluated 22 women in 2024. Of them, two were minors who had been mutilated before arriving in the Valencian Community. Since its creation, the unit has attended to 169 women and girls and has performed 49 surgical interventions for reconstruction to prevent the severe genitourinary and gynecological sequelae that this mutilation causes in many cases. In addition, these women also receive psychosocial assistance as part of the comprehensive care provided by the reference unit. At the moment, there are 26 women being followed up by the team of professionals from the unit, who also have the support of community health agents. Of the women who have attended this reference unit, 36.5% suffered some type of violence in their place of origin, 30.7% had a forced marriage, and 9.6% were victims of human trafficking. Despite the low prevalence in our area, female genital mutilation is still a violation of the human rights of women and girls who are mutilated, and the impact on their health is so important that it is necessary to continue working in this sense and continue training healthcare professionals, said Dr. Reyes BalanzÃ¡, head of the Gynecology Service at the University Hospital Doctor Peset. In occasion of the celebration every February 6th of International Zero Tolerance Day for Female Genital Mutilation, the Committee for Equality and against Gender Violence of the Doctor Peset University Hospital has organized this Wednesday the Female Genital Mutilation marathon. A practice alien to our environment. The meeting has served to make known the reality of women subjected to genital mutilation and the need to prevent new cases in vulnerable minors. Also, the consequences that this practice has at the level of the integral health of these women (physical, psychic, and sexual) and the legal consequences for the families if the minors are mutilated have been exposed. The event was inaugurated by Felipe del BaÃ±o, Commissioner for the Fight against Violence against Women from the First Vice Presidency and Department of Social Services, Equality, and Housing, who was accompanied by Palmira MuÃ±oz, Equality Unit Manager from the Department of Health Luis IbÃ¡Ã±ez, Health Department Manager in Valencia Doctor Peset, and MarÃ­a Amparo Antonaya, Commissioner for Equality and Against Gender Violence from this department. At the event, professionals were informed about their obligations in case of suspected or diagnosed female genital mutilation, the operation of the reference unit at the Doctor Peset University Hospital was explained, and the Protocol for Healthcare Attention in the Face of Female Genital Mutilation was presented. This allows women to receive multidisciplinary care from assistance services. In fact, pediatricians, family and community medicine professionals, gynecologists, obstetricians, midwives, nurses, psychologists, social workers, and public health professionals work together to detect cases, as well as to assess and monitor them according to their specific characteristics.

The Andalusian High Court of Justice (TSJA) has partially upheld the appeal of a man sentenced by the CÃ¡diz Provincial Court to nine years in prison for sex abuse crimes against two nieces of his, committed in Jerez. The high Andalusian court has removed the specific aggravating factor of exploitation, reducing the sentence from nine to six years in prison. The facts, according to the sentence, occurred between 2017 and 2019 when the accused, taking advantage of the fact that his niece's parents, aged 14, were not at home and having the house key due to the existing trust, would visit the residence and take advantage of the situation to commit sexual abuse against the minor, consisting of touching. Similarly, in 2019, he went to the home of another niece, aged 12, to commit similar acts, until the minor managed to escape after insisting that a friend was waiting for her to arrive. Due to these incidents, the defendant was sentenced by the Provincial Court to five years in prison for a sex abuse crime against the first of the nieces and four years for the same crime against the second, so he presented a recourse to the TSJA requesting the annulment of the trial and repetition of another one for violation of the right to a process with all guarantees, insufficiency of the evidence, and non-existence of coercion. On the other hand, the TSJA has dismissed the violation of the right to a process with all guarantees or defenselessness, as well as the insufficiency of the evidence, since it did not find any errors. Notwithstanding, it has estimated the resource of non-prevailing to consider that the uncle-niece relationship was not used for the committed facts, recalling that typical prevailing requires a situation of superiority of the active subject with respect to the passive one that must be taken advantage of by the first to obtain the consent of the second to the realization of the act threatening sexual freedom. Additionally, it notes that prevailing from a relationship of superiority should not be confused with abuse of trust, where the author benefits or favors the calm or relaxation climate generated in the victim as a consequence of the knowledge of the friendly aggressor, of the reasonable hope that the victim has of not being attacked in the context of personal reliability. Thus, the TSJA estimates the part of the appeal in which prevalence is requested and reduces the sentence for sexual abuse to four years for the first of the five nieces and to two years for the second, passing the total sentence to be served from nine to six years.

In this sense, we have border areas that are hotter, where there is greater concern, but if in this way the controls are strengthened in some way, the human, technological, and biometric data resources, then this request for documentation from minors is going to continue being done in order to be authorized to be transported from one place to another. Controversy over this new measure Human rights organizations have expressed their rejection of the measure, arguing that it undermines the protection of children and facilitates the actions of human trafficking networks. The Alameda Foundation, dedicated to fighting exploitation and enslavement, stated in a statement that the elimination of document controls in international transportation represents a setback in the fight against human trafficking, exposing children and adolescents to a greater risk. In the international sphere, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) has expressed concern over the measure and has urged the Argentine government to guarantee the protection of minors.

On February 5, 2025, agents of the National Police arrested four people in Tomelloso (Ciudad Real) as suspected perpetrators of the crimes of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization, managing to liberate seven foreign women in an irregular situation who were being sexually exploited. The victims were forced to engage in prostitution at a brothel run by a foreign woman, who, taking advantage of the vulnerability of the women due to their irregular immigration status, imposed abusive conditions and forced them to engage in prostitution under threats and coercion, keeping the majority of the money they earned from sexual services. The establishment had its own ATM machine. The detained had installed an ATM machine inside the residence so that clients could withdraw money to pay for sexual services without having to leave the brothel. During the entry and search of the premises, over 8,000 euros in cash were found, as well as two phone terminals and various documentation related to the investigation. Additionally, 10 grams of cocaine and 22 grams of marijuana intended for client consumption were also seized. After the arrest of the main suspect, it was confirmed that both she and several family members were engaged in activities aimed at laundering money obtained from the illicit activity of prostitution. In this sense, they sent more than 50,000 euros in several remittances to their country of origin in a few years, created two hospitality companies, and acquired several homes, one of which was donated to a son of the arrested woman to conceal ownership. As a result, three other people from the family circle of the club owner were detained, and all four were charged with the crimes of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization. This operation is part of the National Police's Plan against Human Trafficking for Sexual Exploitation. Sister Martha Pelloni participated in the International Summit on the Rights of Children at the Vatican on Monday, where she denounced the situation of exploitation and violence against children in Argentina and highlighted the Loan case. Pelloni, who during the Menem presidency pushed for the investigation of the case of Maria Soledad in Catamarca and the Marches of Silence, now coordinates the Stolen Childhood Network. At the meeting, held in the Clementine Hall of the Apostolic Palace, she spoke alongside Pope Francis, Queen Rania of Jordan, and authorities from various countries. When taking the floor, the Sister described a critical social context and denounced that in the country, the Universal Declaration of the Rights of the Child has constitutional rank since 1989, but there is a huge gap between the legislation and reality. Today in Argentina, social poverty is structural and is the cause of generating increasingly complex violence in children, Pelloni assured. This does not please the authoritarian ones. The exercise of professional and critical journalism is a fundamental pillar of democracy. That is why it bothers those who believe they are the owners of the truth. Sister Martha Pelloni during the conference at the Vatican While human and social rights are not educated, assumed, and integrated into the states and governments of countries, there will be a lot to fight for from social organizations to make governments defend and implement them, Pelloni indicated without singling out any government but in clear allusion to the current scenario. Pope Francis spoke about the disappearance of Loan and considered the trafficking of organs as one of the hypotheses In his speech, he referred to multiple forms of violation of the rights of children, among which he denounced child sexual exploitation, trafficking, and the sale of organs. Pope Francis mentioned the Loan Case in Corrientes, one of the possibilities of human trafficking, the trade in organs that exists more than we think. It is a business in which clinics and hospitals, especially psychiatric ones, intervene with doctors, nurses, ambulance drivers, police officers, and lawyers. The money that moves is so large that it obliges a greater silence and that's why this topic is not spoken of and it is wanted to be believed that it does not exist, the nun described. Sister Martha Pelloni on the social rights violations of children in Argentina. In the analysis of the country's social situation, Pelloni denounced child labor, the lack of Child Sexual Education (CSI), teenage pregnancy, and poverty. Young unemployed fathers who abuse drugs and physically abuse their children, prompting the state to take their children away and place them in state-run childcare facilities, which have also been accused of abuse on several occasions, stated. He also pointed out that there are children working in shantytowns and neighborhoods who live in vulnerable conditions. Many, from the age of 10, sell drugs, while others consume them and go out to steal. The number of these children not attending school is increasing. Many do not have anyone to care for them. Some attend school but cannot be contained in institutions, with the added aggravation of the loss of values, of parents and teachers who did not set limits and do not know how to do so, he said.New measures and a shocking testimony Children who are not educated about their integral sexuality consume pornography from the age of 9, he stated about the ESI, and added that 12 and 13-year-old girls who become mothers must face an unripe maternity. Finally, the nun referred to child labor and denounced that child labor in the Argentine countryside is another exploited reality. She exemplified that reality with the case of the golondrina workers, who are transported from Bolivia to Argentina for tomato and pepper harvests. They live in the fields of the rich in very poor conditions and suffer from the abuse of pesticides that have caused the deaths of children and birth defects, she claimed. UCA warns that the structural poverty rate is 33%. The Judiciary puts the scales in the defense of the rich. Human dignity, so manipulated by the monetary and capitalist interests of our countries, calls us to fight for what we have come to this encounter for. We join the call of Pope Francis, with the jubilee of this year 2025, to find the path of peace with the hope that does not disappoint, concluded Pelloni. In conclusion, Martha Pelloni also referred to surrogacy, stating that it is not only an exploitation of human life and dignity, but often a gateway to the sale of babies on the internet, a new modality of human trafficking through cyberspace.

text: The militarization of the border will imply risks to the human rights of migrants, anticipates the director of the Centro Prodh, Santiago Aguirre. Santiago Aguirre, director of the Centro Prodh, has expressed concern over the adverse effects on human rights due to the deployment of 10,000 members of the National Guard on the northern border of Mexico, emphasizing the urgency of establishing civilian controls to prevent abuses against migrants. Despite a complicated context with a US government that has demonstrated nativist, racist, and xenophobic tendencies, Aguirre emphasizes the importance of questioning policies that could harm the most vulnerable groups, including migrants. The militarization of the border has shown in practice to put migrant people at risk, he declared, referring to previous deployments since 2019, especially on the southern border of Mexico. Aguirre also mentioned recent incidents where Colombian migrants and others in Chiapas lost their lives, with implications involving the National Guard and the Army. Military intervention in migration matters often results in the excessive and disproportionate use of lethal force against migrants. Without the oversight of the National Human Rights Commission, now aligned with the government, civilian organizations and faith communities have emerged as key figures in denouncing abuses and documenting the human costs of migration policies. It is civilian organizations, faith communities, in short, who are documenting the human cost and the human pain generated by these policies, Aguirre added. Migrant Abuses Migration URL Photo Aristegui Noticias Aguirre also reminded that Mexico has not been a welcoming environment for migrants, pointing out the abuses they suffer, from the disproportionate use of force to extortion and sexual assaults by criminal groups. The militarization not only increases the risks for migrants, but also strengthens human trafficking networks, exacerbating the situation of those crossing the country. Finally, he made a call to civil society, the media, and faith communities to maintain constant vigilance and alert possible abuses. It is very important, now that this deployment is announced, to alert preventively and raise one's voice so that from journalism, from civil society, from faith communities, there can be an alert and, in case, document the cases that are happening. All the Material Was Stored on Their Cellphones.RCN News, 7:23 a.m. Join the RCN News WhatsApp Channel.A Police Operation in Cajamarca, Tolima, Allowed the Rescue of Four Minors Who Were Being Victims of Sexual Exploitation. The Most Alarming Part of the Case Is That Two of the Children Were the Sons of One of the Captors, While the Other Two, Aged 11 and 13, Were Handed Over to the Colombian Institute of Family Welfare (ICBF). The Case Came to Light After the Directorate of Criminal Investigation and Interpol (Dijin) Received Four International Alerts That Confirmed the Existence of Child Abuse Material Distributed Globally. The investigation allowed the perpetrators to be located and confirmed that they were exploiting their roles as fathers and neighbors to abuse minors, record videos, and share them in Colombia and other countries. In addition, according to the information gathered, one of them was the president of the Community Action Board of the El Pedregal neighborhood in Cajamarca, while both had been candidates for municipal council in the 2023 elections. Human trafficking ring discovered in Cajamarca; four minors rescued Colonel Herbert MejÃ­a, who led the procedure, explained how the operation was carried out, allowing the minors to be rescued and evidence to be collected. The operation began with a search and we were able to reach the municipality of Cajamarca in the Tolima. It was there that a search warrant was executed, and we were able to obtain important material evidence, contained in various technological devices. The raid allowed for the confiscation of 17 files containing evidence of the sexual abuse of minors. The recordings were stored on electronic devices seized from the captives and shared with criminal networks dedicated to distributing this type of material. After the capture, the two individuals were presented to a judge, who legalized their detention and imposed a measure of pre-trial detention. A sex trafficking ring in Cajamarca was exposed due to international alerts. For now, the authorities continue with the investigations to determine if there are more victims and if other people are involved in this child sex trafficking ring. However, the evidence gathered so far suggests that the captives not only committed these crimes, but also distributed the material internationally, which led to foreign organizations issuing the alerts that allowed for the discovery. Finally, the rescued children are under the protection of the ICBF, where they will receive specialized care to help them overcome the trauma they suffered.

Reporting cases of Peruvian women and men who are victims of human trafficking and migrant trafficking outside Peru and in Peru Since the enactment of Law 28950, which incorporated the crime of Human Trafficking into the Penal Code, the Ministry of Foreign Relations and other state entities have been developing institutional policies aimed at strengthening the fight against this form of criminality in our country. Joint work is carried out through the Permanent Multisectoral Commission against Human Trafficking and Illicit Migrant Trafficking. Who can report cases of human trafficking and migrant trafficking The victim, family members, friends, or third parties Who is considered a victim of human traffickingA person is considered a victim of human trafficking who, regardless of their race, color, sex, age, language, religion, nationality, political opinion, or any other kind, beliefs, or cultural practices, economic situation, birth, family situation, ethnic or social origin, or physical disability, has suffered harm, including physical or mental injuries, emotional suffering, financial loss, or substantial impairment of fundamental rights, as a consequence of actions or omissions that violate penal legislation. Procedure for Accessing Consular Protection in Cases of Human Trafficking or Migrant SmugglingIf you are a victim, family member, friend, or third party who knows of a Peruvian or Peruvian involved in a case of human trafficking or illicit migrant smuggling abroad, you must report it by contacting the nearest consular office, through the emergency telephone number or email listed on their website, or by visiting in person. Please note that the information you provide will be treated with confidentiality. The Consular Office will inform the competent authority in the receiving country to activate the corresponding actions and the Directorate of Protection and Assistance to Nationals of the Directorate General of Peruvian Communities Abroad and Consular Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Peru, so that it can bring the case to the attention of the Public Ministry. The Consular Office will ensure that the authorities of the receiving country provide the victim of human trafficking with protection, medical attention, psychological care, legal assistance, as well as shelter and material support as required. The victim will be informed by the Consul about their migratory rights, as well as the possibility of being repatriated to Peru, with prior consent. If you know of a case in Peru of Peruvian victims of human trafficking or illicit trafficking of Peruvian migrants abroad, you can report it in the following ways:Through the email of the Ministry of the Interior: denunciasmininter.gob.peThrough the online form of the Public Ministry.Through the 1818 Hotline at the national level. Peruvian Father Rescues Daughter Kidnapped by Aragua Train Gang A 17-year-old Venezuelan girl was rescued in Moquegua, Peru, thanks to the intervention of the Peruvian National Police (PNP) and her father's relentless search. The young woman had been kidnapped by the notorious criminal gang known as Los Hijos de Dios del Tren de Aragua. The ordeal began three weeks ago when the father received an alarming message on social media from his daughter, who managed to send him a brief text that read "I've been kidnapped." According to information from the newspaper El Popular, the kidnappers operated by offering deceitful job opportunities, luring their victims and subjecting them to total control and constant abuse. During her captivity, the teenager had limited access to almost anything, including restricted use of her phone, only to report payments and follow instructions from her captors. In the face of this anguishing situation, the father initiated negotiations with the traffickers through messages while trying to gather the money they were demanding. In a desperate act to save his daughter's integrity, he decided to confront the criminals directly. The Peruvian authorities, particularly the Division Against Human Trafficking, played a crucial role in this case. After conducting an investigation, they located the Dubai Club, a nightclub where several women were being exploited. The law enforcement executed a covert operation, carrying out a raid on the establishment. As a result of this operation, the authorities arrested several members of the criminal gang responsible for the young woman's kidnapping and exploitation. This rescue not only saved the Venezuelan teenager but also paved the way for a broader investigation into the crimes committed by this faction of the criminal organization. text: The victims were forced to engage in prostitution at a brothel run by a foreign woman, who, by exploiting the vulnerability of the women due to their irregular immigration status, imposed abusive conditions and forced them to engage in prostitution under threats and coercion, keeping most of the money they earned from sexual services, as reported by the Police in a press release. The detained woman had installed an ATM machine inside the residence so that clients could withdraw money to pay for sexual services without leaving the brothel. During the entry and search of the premises, over 8,000 euros in cash, two phone terminals, and various documentation related to the investigation were found. Additionally, 10 grams of cocaine and 22 grams of marijuana intended for client consumption were also seized. After the arrest of the main suspect, it was confirmed that both she and several family members were involved in activities aimed at laundering money obtained through the illicit activity of prostitution. In this sense, they sent more than 50,000 euros in several remittances to their country of origin over a few years, created two hospitality companies, and acquired several properties, one of which was donated to the suspect's child to conceal ownership. As a result, three other people from the suspect's family circle have been detained, and all four have been charged with the crimes of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization. This operation is part of the National Police's Plan against Human Trafficking for Sexual Exploitation Purposes. Child Abuse The first year of implementation of the Barnahus model almost triples the detection of child sexual abuse in Catalonia Approximately 2,900 children and adolescents who were victims of sexual assaults visited these centers in 2024 The Government expands the Barnahus program, which has quadrupled the detection of child sexual abuse The 7% of children will suffer sexual abuse before the age of 18, usually in their own home Facilities of the Barnahus center in El Prat de Llobregat.URLACN The first year of implementation of the Barnahus model for the detection and care of child sexual violence in Catalonia is starting to show its first results. In 2024, the year in which the 13 units were opened beyond the pilot project, 2,897 children and adolescents who were victims of sexual assaults visited these centers. If compared to the data managed by the Directorate General for Attention to Childhood and Adolescence, it is a 150% increase, going from 6.6 to 16.5 cases per 10,000 children. This is a good sign because these data were hidden, we are detecting more and achieving that these children are being attended to, explained the general director, Maria Isabel Carrasco. Only half of them have reached the courts. Five years have passed since the Generalitat, following a proposal from Save The Children and after the social emergency caused by the Maristes case, launched a new model of intervention towards sexually abused minors. Catalonia has copied the Scandinavian model, where the affected minor goes to a place and it is there that professionals, from police to judges, passing through healthcare professionals, psychologists or lawyers, coordinate to attend to them in the most sensitive way possible. Additionally, it is in this space that the minor declares before the judge on a screen and at a distance if the family decides to file a complaint. The pilot project, in Tarragona, reached quadrupling the cases detected. Now, the remaining 13 Barnahus are causing a similar impact. Unstoppable Rise The data is still far from the conselleria's predictions, which aimed to reach 3,600 cases per year. It should also be clarified that the last Barnahus opened was the one in Prat de Llobregat (Baix Llobregat) last October, and that in this year, the different teams have been incorporating and forming, that is, it is to be expected that the statistics will increase throughout this year. If compared with the complaints to Mossos in 2022, the 2024 figures represent a 122% increase if compared with the detections through pediatric services two years ago, it is a 300% increase. In any case, the numbers show an unstoppable rise. The main detectors that trigger the alarm are doctors and pediatricians (31%), followed by the child protection system (17%) and schools (14%). By territories, the two Barnahus in Barcelona lead the numbers, with 438 minors attended, followed by Girona, with 317 cases, Terrassa, with 301, and Tarragona, with 303. The Seu d'Urgell and Tortosa, the two least populated territories, have detected 64 and 102 cases respectively. According to the data revealed this Thursday by the Conselleria de Drets Socials, half of the abuse occurs at the hands of relatives (53.1%), and 49% is perpetrated by outsiders to the home, caregivers, teachers, monitors, or even adolescent children. The cases within the family are the most complex and least reported, it is essential that they start to arrive, the general director insisted. Violent Acts Among AdolescentsAlthough there are between 100 and 200 children treated in each age range, the majority profile is that of a girl (78%), adolescent (42%). Carrasco has acknowledged that a part of the aggressors are adolescent boys of the same age, although he has not provided data. The minors who commit these acts are not treated at Barnahus, but are instead sent to juvenile violence programs or those for minors who are not criminally responsible, depending on whether they are under or over 14 years old and are reported to a judge. Only half of them report it.Our commitment is to eradicate this scourge and protect childhood. There can be no impunity, and it is essential that affected families receive support and do not feel alone, and can take the step forward for cases to come to light, the counselor emphasized. The data provided reveal that only half of the minors treated have initiated a penal procedure. However, the Government has not provided data on how many pre-established trials have been instructed, how many minors are receiving psychological or medical attention, or what effect it has had on the sentences. In some cases, they are still not prepared to initiate the legal process, Carrasco has pointed out, adding that the attention is individualized and a response is not delayed for more than a month. The procedure is that within a week, the territorial committee decides the plan to be followed in each case and it is implemented, making a tailored suit for each minor, Carrasco insisted. The counselor explained that they are conducting an external audit to detect possible errors or improvements, although she emphasized that, as of today, the balance is positive. This year, they have received visits from all over the world to learn how the model is applied. The Government and several autonomous communities, such as the Basque Country or Navarre, have shown interest in it. Members of the Council of Europe, the Government of Andorra, Chile, or Argentina have also visited. Interest has also been shown from Ireland or Japan. This year, the Govern will study deploying a regulation to govern this service, update the protocol against child violence, and propose to bet on preventive policies.

The United States notified the United Nations that it will freeze funds destined for a mission supported by the UN in Haiti that is in charge of combating gangs that are trying to take total control of the Caribbean nation's capital, the organization reported on Tuesday. The United States has been the largest contributor to the mission led by the Kenyan police, which was launched last year and is struggling with a lack of funding and personnel. The interruption will have an immediate impact on the mission, noted Stephane Dujarric, a UN spokesperson. The United States had committed to allocating $15 million to the fiduciary fund that finances the multinational force, he said. After $1.7 million of that had already been spent, $13.3 million has now been frozen, Dujarric commented. The measure comes into effect as US President Donald Trump imposes a blanket freeze on foreign aid, leading to the dismissal of thousands of employees and contractors from US aid agencies and the closure of programs worldwide. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has offered an exemption for life-saving programs, but the confusion over what is exempt from the suspension orders and the fear of losing US aid permanently continues to freeze aid and development work globally. The funding interruption seemed to catch Kenyan mission leaders off guard. When asked for comment, the mission's spokesperson, Jack Mbaka, declined to make any immediate reaction. The mission works alongside the Haitian National Police, which suffers from severe shortages of funds and personnel, and has received millions of dollars from the US government in recent years to help combat gangs. Currently, there are only around 4,000 Haitian police officers on duty at any given time in a country of over 11 million inhabitants. The announcement was made just hours after a contingent of 70 Salvadoran soldiers arrived in Haiti, joining over 600 Kenyan police officers already on the ground and backed by police and soldiers from other countries, including Jamaica and Guatemala. It is unclear what impact the interruption of US funding for the mission could have on efforts to transform it into a UN peacekeeping mission. The international security mission in Haiti was already facing very significant challenges and was severely understaffed. With this withdrawal of aid, their work there will become even more difficult, noted Michael Deibert, author of the texts about the Caribbean nation Notes From the Last Testament The Struggle for Haiti and Haiti Will Not Perish A Recent History. The suspension of funds occurs in the midst of an unrelenting attack by hundreds of gang members in a high-end neighborhood of the capital Port-au-Prince that began over a week ago and has left at least 40 dead. The gangs already control 85 percent of the capital, and the UN Secretary-General, AntÃ³nio Guterres, recently warned that they could take over Port-au-Prince entirely if additional support is not provided to the multinational force. Last year, over 5,600 homicides were reported throughout Haiti, and more than 2,200 people were injured. The gang violence has left over a million people homeless in recent years, according to the UN. The situation in Haiti is unprecedented in its gravity, said Diego Da Rin, crisis analyst for the International Crisis Group. Dujarric noted that a recent UN human rights report on Haiti reiterated concerns about the ongoing sexual exploitation and abuse of women and girls by gang members, and the recruitment of children into gangs.

On Wednesday, February 5, in the municipality of Cajamarca, Tolima, two individuals were apprehended, apparently involved in the production, storage, and distribution of child sexual abuse material. The National Government, through Decree 5XXXX, officially abolished the requirement for international transportation companies to ask for a National Identity Document (DNI) from minors for verification. This measure has generated strong criticism, as it represents a significant change in the regulation of the transfer of children and adolescents, rendering ineffective a key regulation aimed at preventing cases of child trafficking and kidnapping. On our radio program 103.7 FM MÃ¡s, we discussed this topic with Silvina Calveyra, coordinator of the Provincial Council Against Human Trafficking, who told us the following:Today, we had communication with authorities from the National Council Against Human Trafficking at the national level, of which we are a part, and also with Migration authorities in order to interpret and understand a bit the resolution, because that's what it's about. In this sense, and personally, it's not good to remove controls, especially when it comes to children, girls, and adolescents under the age of 18. However, we must also understand that many times private companies, primarily land-based internationally, do not perform the necessary controls either. This resolution deals with a matter of functionality towards the sale of tickets, towards companies, but it does not negate the fact that officials from the Directorate of Migrations are responsible for controlling the documentation of minors. In this sense, we have border zones that are hotter, where there is greater concern, but if controls are somehow strengthened, human, technological, and biometric data resources, then this request for documentation from minors will continue to be made in order to be authorized to be transported from one place to another. Controversies over this new measure Human rights organizations have expressed their rejection of the measure, arguing that it undermines the protection of childhood and facilitates the actions of human trafficking networks. The Alameda Foundation, dedicated to fighting exploitation and slavery, stated in a statement that the elimination of document controls in international transportation represents a step back in the fight against human trafficking, exposing children and adolescents to a greater risk. In the international arena, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) has expressed concern over the measure and has urged the Argentine government to ensure the protection of minors.
