text: Online communities dedicated to the sexual abuse of children and the manipulation of vulnerable minors for the commission of violent crimes are under the spotlight of law enforcement agencies, Europol reports. The coercion to commit violent crimes includes various possibilities, such as acts of cruelty against people and animals, murders, and self-harm. These groups belong to a larger online network known as The Com. Through this network, gangs operate virtually in easily accessible spaces, such as social media platforms, mobile applications, and online gaming platforms. International cooperation with Europol has intensified in recent times, allowing for the identification of dangerous individuals and the protection of victims, mostly vulnerable minors. Arrests in the United StatesOn January 30, U.S. National Security detained two individuals for participating in a neo-Nazi child exploitation ring that prepared and coerced minors into producing child abuse material and self-harm images. At least 16 minors were exploited worldwide. According to the investigation, the two men were members of CVLT, a band promoting neo-Nazism, nihilism, and pedophilia as core principles. Europol and the French Police also participated in the investigation. Members of the violent CVLT community prepared minors to produce child abuse material through various methods, including exposing victims to extreme and violent content. CVLT specifically targeted vulnerable victims, including minors with mental health issues or histories of sexual abuse. They encouraged the victims to participate in acts such as cutting and eating their own hair, drinking their own urine, hitting themselves, racially insulting themselves, and using razors to carve the names of CVLT members into their skin. Live Suicide The coercion by CVLT members reached such an extreme that they pressured the victims to commit suicide through a live video. They blackmailed the victims into submitting and keeping quiet, threatening to distribute compromising photos and videos of their families and friends. On occasion, CVLT has carried out its threats against victims who tried to escape their clutches. The predators prepare their victims through various methods, one of which involves establishing friendships based on trust or romantic relationships. Another technique involves using power or coercive tactics solely to gain control over the victims. This is a vicious cycle, as the perpetrators of this network influence children or young people to commit acts that humiliate, incriminate, or isolate them further, making them more vulnerable to further exploitation.

In Spain, a study conducted by the ANAR Foundation between 2008 and 2019 found that nearly 60% of victims are girls, with a higher incidence at ages 5 and 15, and that the most common perpetrator is the father. Additionally, this study indicates that 5% of abuse cases are detected by professionals in the educational field and estimates that more than half of known cases of sexual abuse do not get reported. The City Council of AlcorcÃ³n launched a Technical Commission on Sexual Violence in Childhood and Adolescence months ago to work against these sexual abuses, as part of its involvement with childhood. This commission, dependent on the Local Council for the Rights of Childhood and Adolescence of AlcorcÃ³n, has been working on a project of multidisciplinary and inter-institutional intervention for the detection and prevention of child sexual abuse in recent months. Detecting child sexual abuse from schools Now, it has launched a new formative project to detect situations of sexual violence towards children and adolescents from educational centers, in line with what the FundaciÃ³n ANAR study highlighted. In the face of this situation of child vulnerability, we believe it is necessary to raise awareness and sensitize the different professionals about child sexual abuse, highlighted the Councilor for Social Services and Disability, Pilar JimÃ©nez, one of the driving forces behind this Technical Commission against child sexual abuse. The Commission's current focus is to provide training to professionals from various fields, especially in educational centers, with the aim of working with the educational community to develop prevention strategies and provide them with tools for detecting and reporting potential cases. The Councillor for Social Services and Disability, Pilar JimÃ©nez, one of the driving forces behind this Technical Commission against child sexual abuse in AlcorcÃ³n, has implemented a successful pilot project. Last year, this initiative was developed as a pilot project in three Primary Education centers and two Nursery Schools, where 153 teachers participated, and it will be extended to all educational centers in the municipality in the first semester of 2025. This activity consists of a formative session, through didactic material constructed jointly and collaboratively by the institutions participating in the Commission (Social Services, Primary Health Care, Education Guidance Team, and Early Intervention Team), on how to detect these child sexual abuses. Detained victims of exploitation Four detained and 52 victims liberated from labor exploitation The Civil Guard of Seville has liberated 52 people who were being exploited laboriously and has detained four suspected members of a criminal network in an operation framed in the Plan of Fight against Human Trafficking. This group operated for several years in the locality of Brenes and extended its criminal activity throughout the province of Seville. The investigation was carried out by the Woman-Minor Unit of the Civil Guard (Emume) of the Judicial Police of the Command of Seville, according to a press release. The authors caught the victims through job advertisements published on Romanian social networks, offering false job opportunities in Spain. Once they had contacted them by phone, they promised legal working conditions, competitive salaries, free housing, and free transportation. However, upon arrival in Spain, the victims were taken to homes located in Brenes and nearby towns, where they lived in extreme unsanitary conditions. Additionally, they were imposed an abusive debt for transportation costs, despite the fact that this had been offered as free. When she was 9 years old, Jessica Martinelli was sexually abused by a family friend in the Brazilian town of ChapecÃ³. The situation lasted for nearly two and a half years. At 15, she reported her abuser and only at 25, now a police officer, was she able to apprehend him. The 33-year-old woman recounted the experience in a book she published at the end of 2024 in Brazil, A Calha. It's a story that I know really motivates victims to report, to tell their stories. Besides bringing some justice because many victims tell me that my action in some way brought them comfort. Because many of them no longer have the means to detain their aggressor, the woman said in an interview with the g1 website. In the book, Jessica recounts that the abuse occurred when she was between 9 and 11 and a half years old, and only ceased after the friendship between the aggressor and her family was broken. The man was 33 years old when the crimes began. When she was 15, Jessica managed to tell her sister about the abuse she suffered and together they went to the police station to file a complaint. However, according to her, it was very difficult to get the authorities to take the case seriously. She had to repeat the same thing thousands of times, she lamented. She believes that everything that happened to her in her childhood led her to choose a career in law enforcement. She looked at photos of female police officers and saw something she really wanted to have, which was strength. That strength, that courage, sustained her. It's not that I joined the police to catch my abuser. Because I wouldn't have imagined that the process would take 10 years. It's just that things happened that way, she assured, although she emphasized that being in the force allowed her to drive the cause forward. Let it be clear that things happened because I was pushing things forward, she stated. The sex abuser was arrested on December 22, 2016. Jessica participated in the operation. It was like she was 11 years old again. I was on the patrol car, but I had a mix of courage. I'm a police officer, I'm here to arrest the person who did it and at the same time, I felt a tremor, a lot of anxiety, fear. I don't know, fear that they would do something to me, remembered the moment of the arrest. My colleagues checked him, but I was the one who locked the cell door. And it was really like the end of a 10-year cycle. A very painful cycle, one that no victim should have to go through.

The religious organization is involved in a judicial case for human trafficking and another that investigates the fate of one of the great fortunes in Latin America. Paula Bistagnino's investigation. Author. Bistagnino's book is the result of years of methodical work. Its content is key in at least two judicial cases. Photo Alejandra LÃ³pez The Opus Dei is a power-seeking organization, but it pretends to do so without anyone noticing. Those who know it very well, those who were inside, those who held positions of hierarchy speak of an opaque institution, if not directly, fraudulent for its own members and even for the Catholic Church. Also for the States and democracies. Because the Work does not follow democratic rules in general, notes journalist Paula Bistagnino, author of Te servirÃ©. Fe, poder y disciplina (Planeta), a documented and incisive book based on years of research and whose content is key in at least two judicial cases. In one of the lawsuits, 43 women accuse the religious organization of human trafficking, forced servitude, and labor exploitation, a series of episodes that allegedly took place in a maids' school, and it must answer for the trail of one of the largest family fortunes in Latin America, whose path dissolves near civic associations linked to the Work. You can read it as a suspense story, but it's the narration of real paths, of lives, of people whose direction changed radically after the Opus Dei crossed their path, in its successful attempt to extend itself to Latin America, once the shoots flourished in Spanish soil under the sun of the Franco regime. Father Bistagnino reports that in the 1950s, one of the first priests sent by the founder JosemarÃ­a EscrivÃ¡ de Balaguer for the Work to take root in Latin America discovered in Chile the Gianoli Gainza family, who had made their fortune through mining. The spark was instantaneous. The ties between Opus Dei and the matriarch first and her children later became intimate. All became members, the youngest daughter, Elina, did so as a teenager, with such fervor that she spent the rest of her life fulfilling vows of chastity, poverty, and obedience. She, who died in 2021 in Argentina, was unknown to outsiders, but behind closed doors, her name was synonymous with sanctity and vocation. As a benefactress, she was the most important woman in the feminine branch in Argentina, where she arrived with the mission of supporting and multiplying thanks to her donation, which had arrived in Rome, at the names of the important, within that opaque world. She died, allegedly, in poverty, her nephews accused the Opus Dei of hiding more than her precarious health. Since 2016, Uruguayan courts have been investigating whether certain numeraries operated in the shadows to intervene in the family's finances and deprive them of their inheritance. The book also tells in detail another story: that of poor young women who were taken far from their families with the promise of education and dignified work, but who ended up enslaved. That systematic operation turned them into auxiliary numeraries. They were girls who were formed in the maids' school. They were convinced that divine will wanted them to be servants and not of just anyone, but of the elite people who were part of the Opus Dei. Today, they are known as The 43, because that is the number of women who managed to escape and, after a long time, find each other and begin to claim judicially a path in which Bistagnino's investigation played a key role. The case could have implications beyond Argentine borders. For years, the school for maids was a rumor surrounding the centers of Opus Dei. Elina Gianoli Gainza's existence, on the other hand, was closer to a legend. That's why telling her story was the most difficult part of the investigation. It was the story of a woman about whom there was no public record because her life had taken place behind walls. I was already perfectly familiar with Opus Dei's modus operandi, but I needed to find witnesses that would allow me to reconstruct that life, and recount the way Opus Dei acted in that life, in that family, and at that time, Bistagnino says. There was another step beyond accepting speaking, witnesses had to accept doing it in a book. It was the most difficult part. Even more than checking data or finding some information, the journalist recalls. Revealing secrets is not free. In addition to the fear of exposure in front of an apparently powerful organization, in some cases, a difficult-to-predict family dimension is added. There are people who have a greater commitment because their families belong to Opus Dei, because they still have people within Opus Dei, and that has personal implications. Several of them feel that those other people often didn't care about how badly they were treated or the harm they were caused in some cases, even questioning whether they left Opus Dei. I think, in some way, the possibility of giving testimony makes those people today say to the person I am concerned about: if before you didn't care about my pain, now I'm not going to worry about the impact my story will have, it's my story and I have the right to tell the truth. The book by Bistagnino, the reopening of the case for human trafficking and labor exploitation, and the progress of the investigation into the Gianoli Gainza inheritance, is also added to the publication of another book about The Work, Opus. Sixty years of a conspiracy backed by money and religion, by Gareth Gore, a British journalist whom Bistagnino met while working on separate stories. It is unusual in its entire existence, the Opus Dei moved in the shadows, and even though its movements were grandiose and ostentatious, they were not usually the subject of investigation. I was surprised when I started working and realized that many things were there, not so hidden, yet they had not been the subject of journalistic investigation, Bistagnino recognizes. Not to mention judicial or academic investigations, no. I don't have an answer as to what kept it hidden in that way. I'm not sure if it's the impunity itself, the numerous ramifications and tentacles it has. In some cases, because in some media outlets they were more papist than the Pope and rejected publishing things about the topic, but well, in any case, it remained there as a kind of vacuum that I found very productive, as I found a topic that appeared only laterally or through a character or through an institution and so on. Up to now, in fact, in Latin America, the Opus Dei was still functioning as an impune and untouchable power. When the publication of Te servirÃ© was announced, the Opus Dei representation in Argentina referred to the editorial novelty with a statement titled In response to false information published in the book Te servirÃ© by Paula Bistagnino, in which, unexpectedly even for the litigating heirs and for the judicial cause, the organization revealed that, in reality, the disputed testament of legitimacy had been revoked.

The measure was published in the Official Gazette through Decree 5URL, by means of which the National Government officially eliminated the obligation for transportation companies to verify the documentation of minors before allowing their boarding on international services. Through Resolution 1URL, published on January 30 in the Official Gazette, the National Government eliminated the obligation of transportation companies to verify the documentation of minors on international trips. The measure was adopted by the Ministry of Infrastructure, within the framework of the deregulation policy being implemented by the administration of Javier Milei. Article one of the Resolution derogates Article five of Resolution 43URL of the National Commission for Transportation Regulation (Cnrt), which established that international passenger transportation companies had to demand the corresponding documentation of minors before boarding. In particular, the repealed regulation required companies to verify the identity of minors and the authorization of parents or guardians to travel, thus preventing possible irregularities in the transport of children and adolescents. This resolution has already taken effect, which means that transportation companies are no longer required to request or verify these documents before boarding. In response to this measure, criticisms from the opposing sector were not long in coming, as it generated concern in various sectors, as it could facilitate cases of human trafficking and irregular transfers of minors without the consent of their legal guardians.

Brenes Trafficking Ring Busted A criminal gang dedicated to human trafficking has been dismantled in Brenes. The perpetrators lured their victims through job ads published on Romanian social media platforms, promising false job opportunities in Spain. The Civil Guard in Seville, as part of the Human Trafficking Prevention Plan of the General Directorate of the Civil Guard, has dismantled a group of human traffickers exploiting people for labor purposes. This group operated for several years in the town of Brenes and extended its illicit activities throughout the province of Seville. The investigation, carried out by the Women-Minors Unit (EMUME) of the Judicial Police of the Seville Command, has led to the arrest of four suspected members of the criminal group, rescuing 52 people who were exploited for labor purposes, and identified as victims of human trafficking for labor exploitation purposes. The authors lured the victims through job advertisements posted on Romanian social media, promising false job opportunities in Spain. Once they contacted them by phone, they promised legal working conditions, competitive salaries, free accommodation and transportation. However, upon arrival in Spain, the victims were taken to homes located in Brenes and nearby towns, where they lived in extreme unsanitary conditions. Additionally, they were imposed an abusive debt for transportation costs, despite this being offered as free. To control the victims, the traffickers confiscated their passports, restricted their movements, and forced them to work endless shifts in the collection of field crops, receiving salaries much lower than those established by Spanish labor conventions, with some cases experiencing threats and physical aggression. In addition, the workers were not registered with Social Security.

text: The Civil Guard has dismantled, as part of Operation MATE, a criminal organization established in the provinces of Tarragona and CastellÃ³n dedicated to the trafficking of human beings for the purpose of sexual exploitation and has released nine victims. In total, a 37-year-old woman and a 32-year-old man, leaders of the organization, as well as four other members of the criminal group, have been detained, according to a statement from the Civil Guard, who initiated this operation at the beginning of 2024 after becoming aware that in several locations in Alcanar and Vinaroz there were women being sexually exploited.During the investigation, it was confirmed that prostitution was being exercised in a premises and in a private residence by several women who were offering sexual services without having a labor contract or the necessary documentation to reside legally in Spain. It was also confirmed that these women had their freedom of movement severely limited. The agents found out that when these women had to be transported to another place where they were also exploited, they were accompanied at all times by members of the criminal organization. Similarly, according to the cited statement, some of the victims lived in the same places where they were forced to engage in prostitution, living in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions. The criminal network exercised strict control over them, both with personnel acting as guards and with video surveillance systems installed in their own homes. The criminal organization used internet pages dedicated to offering sexual services as the main means to attract clients. With the profits from this activity, the members of the organization had also acquired 80 tenths of a lottery ticket for the Christmas draw to launder the hypothetical prize. In parallel, investigations are being conducted into possible money transfers from human trafficking activities to Latin America. InvestigationDuring the first phase of Operation MATE, the two leaders were detained and three properties in Alcanar and Vinaroz were searched, resulting in the seizure of 6,270 euros, computer devices with information on the recruitment of women, documentation, as well as notes on the services provided and payments received from the victims. During the second phase, four additional members of the criminal organization were identified, responsible for logistics and the transportation of women to the locations where they were exploited. They also transported women arriving in Spain under the false promise of a job contract, transferring them to the locations where they were to be exploited.

In Colorado, when an employee or volunteer at a correctional institution engages in sexual conduct with an inmate, they commit the crime of sexual misconduct in a correctional institution. This crime can be charged as a misdemeanor or felony, depending on the accused's position and the type of sexual conduct. Sexual conduct in a correctional institution also results in being designated as a sex offender. In this article, our Colorado criminal defense attorneys will address 1. What is sexual misconduct in a correctional institution. An employee, contracted employee, or volunteer of a correctional institution or a person performing work or volunteer functions in a correctional institution who engages in sexual conduct with a person under lawful custody in a correctional institution commits the crime of sexual misconduct in a correctional institution. .1 A correctional institution refers to any government facility in which individuals can be legally detained as a result of a conviction for a crime. This includes correctional facilities operated under contract with the Department of Corrections, privately contracted prisons, jails, juvenile detention centers, or community correctional program facilities.2 Sexual misconduct in a correctional institution involves workers or volunteers who engage in sexual acts with inmates. This includes sexual misconduct committed for arousal, gratification, or sexual abuse. Regardless of whether the inmate consented to the sexual activity, it remains illegal for employees, contracted employees, or volunteers to participate in sexual activity with an inmate. 2. What types of sexual misconduct are included Sexual misconduct includes sexual contact, intrusion, or penetration.3 According to the CRS 183401, sexual contact includes touching a person's intimate parts or the clothing that covers the immediate area of a person's intimate parts with the purpose of excitement, gratification, or sexual abuse. Intimate parts include external genitals, the perineum, the anus, buttocks, the pubic area, or the breasts of any person. Sexual penetration includes coitus, cunnilingus, fellatio, anilingus, or anal coitus. Sexual penetration does not require proof of ejaculation or any emission as an element of sexual penetration. Any penetration, no matter how small or brief, is considered sexual penetration. All other intrusions by an object or body part with the purpose of sexual excitement or gratification are considered sexual intrusion. 3 The Penalties Sexual conduct in a correctional institution can be a serious crime or a minor crime, depending on the circumstances. Sexual conduct in a correctional institution is a serious crime of class 5 if it includes sexual intrusion or penetration and is committed by an employee or contracted employee. The penalties for a conviction for a serious crime of class 5 for sexual conduct in a correctional institution include 12 to 18 months in prison and a fine of up to $200,000. There is also a mandatory two-year period of probation. Sexual conduct in a correctional institution is a serious crime of class 6 if it consisted only of sexual conduct and there was no intrusion or penetration by an employee. It is also a serious crime of class 6 if it involves sexual intrusion or penetration committed by a volunteer. Punishments for a conviction of a class 6 felony for sex offense in a correctional institution include 12 to 18 months in prison and a fine of up to $100,000. There is also mandatory supervised probation for 1 year. If a volunteer commits a sex offense without sexual intrusion or penetration, it is a class 1 misdemeanor. Punishments for a sex offense in a correctional institution include up to 364 days in jail and up to $1,000 in fines. 4. I Have to Register as a Sex Offender A conviction for a sex offense in a correctional institution results in being designated as a sex offender, and their name will be entered into the Colorado Bureau of Investigation's sex offender registry. As a sex offender, the person must register with the local police chief or county sheriff in any jurisdiction where they reside. The sex offender registry includes providing the sex offender's name, date of birth, address, place of employment, fingerprints, a photograph, email addresses, and identities of instant messaging or chat rooms. The sex offender will also have to re-register annually, every year within 5 days of their birthday. Sex offenders must also re-register each time they change their address or begin working at an institution of higher education. Not registering as a sex offender or knowingly providing false information is a crime in Colorado. The penalties for not registering as a sex offender depend on whether the person was convicted of a minor or major sex offense. Not registering as a sex offender for a minor sex offense is a class 1 misdemeanor. Not registering for a major sex offense is a class 6 felony. Crimes related to Invasion of Privacy for Sexual Gratification C.R.S. 18-3-405.6 Taking intimate photos of people without their consent for sexual gratification can be a misdemeanor or felony, depending on the defendant's criminal history and the victim's age. It is also an extraordinary risk crime. A conviction for invasion of privacy for sexual gratification can result in up to 2 years in prison, a fine of up to $100,000, and classification as a sex offender.Indecent Exposure C.R.S. 18-7-302 Exposing one's genitals to another person is considered indecent exposure and a violation of Colorado law. Masturbating in public is also considered indecent exposure. Indecent exposure is a class 1 misdemeanor in Colorado and can result in up to 364 days in custody and a fine of $1,000. A conviction for indecent exposure will also require registration as a sex offender.Indecent Conduct C.R.S. 18-7-201 Engaging in indecent conduct, including but not limited to, engaging in any of the following acts in a public place or in a place where others are present and might be offended or alarmed, is a class 3 misdemeanor: (a) Exposing one's anus or genitals in a manner that is open and viewable to the public;(b) Masturbating in a public place or in a place where others are present and might be offended or alarmed;(c) Engaging in any of the above acts with another person in a public place or in a place where others are present and might be offended or alarmed;(d) Engaging in any of the above acts in a manner that is likely to be viewed by a child under the age of 16. 187302 Exposing one's intimate parts, engaging in public sex, or exposing one's genitals to offend another person is a violation of Colorado's public indecency law. Public indecency is a petty offense. A conviction for public indecency could result in up to 10 days in jail and/or up to $300 in fines.Lewd Conduct C.R.S. 187301 Lewd conduct involves exposing one's genitals, engaging in public sex, or masturbating in public, or touching another person in a lewd manner, which is a violation of Colorado's public indecency and indecent exposure laws. Penalties for lewd conduct depend on whether the conduct is charged as public indecency or indecent exposure.Criminal Trespass C.R.S. 184502 A person commits criminal trespass in Colorado when they enter or remain on the property of another without permission. Intrusion can be of first, second, or third degree, depending on the type of property involved and the reason for entering or remaining on the property. Penalties for criminal trespass in Colorado range from a fine and probation to three years in prison and a fine of $100,000. Legal references C.R.S. 187701. The language of the law states the following:(1) An employee, contracted employee, or volunteer of a correctional institution or a person performing work or volunteer functions in a correctional institution who engages in sexual conduct with a person under legal custody in a correctional institution commits the offense of sexual conduct in a correctional institution.(2) For the purposes of this section (a) Correctional institution means a correctional facility, as defined in section 171102(1.7), C.R.S., a local jail, as defined in section 171102(7), C.R.S. Operated by or under contract with the department of corrections, a prison, an installation operated by or under contract with the department of human services in which minors are or may be detained legally for detention or commitment for the commission of a crime, or a facility of a community corrections program as defined in section 17-2710.2(3), C.R.S. (b) Sexual conduct means sexual contact as defined in section 18-3-401(4), sexual intrusion as defined in section 18-3-401(5), or sexual penetration as defined in section 18-3-401(6). Sexual conduct does not include acts by an employee of a correctional institution or a person having custody of another person that are performed to carry out the necessary functions of the employee or person with custody. (3) Sexual behavior in a correctional institution is a Class 5 felony if the sexual behavior includes sexual intrusion or sexual penetration and is committed by an employee or contractor of a correctional institution or by an employee, contractor, or person performing work functions in a correctional institution for the Department of Corrections, the Department of Human Services, or a community corrections program. (4) Sexual conduct in a correctional institution is a class 6 felony if (a) The sexual conduct consists solely of sexual contact and is committed by an employee or contractor of a correctional institution or by an employee, contractor, or person performing work in a correctional institution or for the Department of Corrections, the Department of Human Services, or a community corrections program (b) The sexual conduct includes sexual intrusion or penetration and is committed by a volunteer. (5) Sexual conduct in a correctional institution is a class 1 misdemeanor if the sexual conduct consists solely of sexual contact and is committed by a volunteer. CIUDAD REAL, 5 Feb. (EUROPA PRESS) National Police agents have detained four people in Tomelloso (Ciudad Real) as suspected perpetrators of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization, freeing seven foreign women in an irregular situation who were being sexually exploited. The victims were forced to engage in prostitution in a brothel run by a foreign woman, who, taking advantage of the women's vulnerability due to their irregular situation, imposed abusive conditions and forced them to engage in prostitution under threats and coercion, keeping most of the money they earned for sexual services, according to a police press release. The detained individual had installed an ATM inside the residence so that clients could withdraw money to pay for sex services without leaving the brothel. During the entry and search of the premises, over 8,000 euros in cash, two phone terminals, and various documentation related to the investigation were found. Additionally, 10 grams of cocaine and 22 grams of marijuana intended for client consumption were seized. Following the arrest of the main suspect, it was found that both she and several family members were involved in money laundering activities related to the illicit prostitution business. Specifically, they sent more than 50,000 euros in several remittances to their country of origin over a few years, established two hospitality companies, and acquired various properties, including one that was donated to the suspect's child to conceal ownership. As a result of these events, three more people from the family circle of the club's owner have been detained, and all four have been charged with the crimes of prostitution, drug trafficking, money laundering, and membership in a criminal organization. This operation is part of the National Police's Plan against Human Trafficking for Sexual Exploitation. The National Police has a hotline at 900 10 50 90 and the email address tratapolicia.es to facilitate citizen collaboration and anonymous and confidential reporting of this type of crime, with the call not appearing on the phone bill.

text: A criminal network operating in the town of Brenes, in the province of Seville, has been dismantled by the Civil Guard, freeing 52 people who were being exploited laboriously. Four suspected members of this network have been detained in an operation that is part of the Plan to Combat Human Trafficking. The investigation, carried out by the Women-Minors Unit of the Civil Guard (Emume) of the Judicial Police of the Command of Seville, has revealed that the accused recruited the victims through job ads on social media in Romania, promising them legal working conditions, competitive salaries, free accommodation, and transportation. However, upon arriving in Spain, the exploited people were taken to homes in Brenes and nearby towns, where they lived in deplorable conditions. They were imposed an abusive debt for the costs of transportation, despite being promised that the transportation would be free. To maintain control over the victims, the detained individuals confiscated their passports, restricted their movements, and forced them to work long hours in agricultural fruit harvesting, receiving salaries below the minimum wage established by Spanish law. Furthermore, the workers were not registered with the Social Security system, and in some cases, they suffered threats and physical aggression.

Six years in prison for sexually abusing his nieces, minors, in Jerez The TSJA reduces by three years the sentence imposed by the Provincial Court, considering that the aggravating factor of superiority cannot be applied The Supreme Court rejects the appeal of the father and uncle of a minor they sexually assaulted in Jerez The Superior Court of Justice of Andalusia (TSJA) has reduced the prison sentence imposed on a Jerez resident who sexually abused two of his nieces, both minors. The Provincial Court initially imposed a nine-year prison sentence for two sexual abuse crimes, one of which was continuous. However, after the convicted person presented an appeal, the high court reduced this time by three years, determining that the aggravating factor of superiority should not be applied, as he took advantage of his position as uncle of the victims to commit the crimes. The Andalusian high court considers proven that Francisco R. R. abused his nieces between 2015 and 2018, when they were between 10 and 13 years old. The sexual abuse was committed by one of the victims, who suffered it between the ages of 14 and 16, and the other at the age of 12 on one occasion. In this sense, it supports the conclusions of the ruling of the Eighth Section of the Provincial Court. In the same way that the provincial court did, it confirms the main incriminating evidence, the statements of the minors, as it meets all the valuation criteria established by case law for this type of case, such as the absence of subjective incredibility (a motive for revenge or resentment in the complaint), the persistence in incrimination, and the existence of external corroborating data. Additionally, it emphasizes that their testimonies were corroborated by the psychological reports carried out during the investigation of the case, which concluded that there was no reason for the victims to make false accusations, and classified their testimonies as probably true. To this, the testimony of some witnesses was added who claimed during the oral hearing that the defendant confessed the criminal facts once they became public. In the appeal, the TSJA rejects the defendant's exculpatory arguments, but, however, does accept the one related to the aggravating circumstance that was applied for the penalty calculation, specifically the one of exploitation for having used the relationship of uncle and niece to commit the facts for which the defendant was convicted. The high court reasons that jurisprudence establishes that exploitation occurs when there is a manifest situation of inferiority of the victim over the defendant that restricts their capacity to decide freely and the other deliberately takes advantage of their position of superiority. In this sense, the Tribunal warns that this situation of superiority must be described in the sentence in a rational manner by the judicial body that issues the ruling. In this case, it argues that the reasoning is not sufficient because the jurisprudence establishes that the relationship of kinship or the age difference is not a simple reason to apply it. In this way, the TSJA concludes that the convicted person must be punished with six years and one day in prison for two sexual abuse crimes, one of which is continuous in nature. However, the accessory penalties will not be modified, once the prison sentence is served, the convicted person must comply with an order of separation from the victims, 10 and 9 years old, respectively, and must compensate them with 6,000 euros each. The sentence is not final and can be appealed in cassation to the Supreme Court.

Seven years ago, on February 3, the disappearance of Candela Agustina De Melo, a 15-year-old girl who left her home in San Vicente and was never seen again, was commemorated. San Vicente Informa spoke with her father, Pablo Correa De Melo, who assured that he has not lowered his arms in his relentless search and continues to demand that the case be investigated by the Federal Justice, under the suspicion that his daughter may have been a victim of a human trafficking network. Candela disappeared on the night of February 3, 2018, when she left her home to supposedly meet her boyfriend, Carlos Da Silva, a 20-year-old young man who lived in Agro Forestal, about 20 kilometers from her home. At that time, her mother, Nilda Galeano, reported that Candela was carrying a backpack with a change of clothes and had confessed to being 11 weeks pregnant. However, since that night, nothing was known about her again. Candela's boyfriend was arrested days after her disappearance, but was released due to the lack of conclusive evidence against him. Although he has always been considered a suspect, the investigation has not advanced enough to clarify what happened to the young woman. Pablo Correa De Melo, who has dedicated the last seven years to searching for his daughter, insists that the case must be reopened and transferred to the Federal Justice, as he believes Candela could have been a victim of a human trafficking network. A stalled investigation Pablo Correa De Melo has held meetings with provincial senators and local authorities to request support in the investigation. Throughout these years, the investigation has been marked by the lack of significant progress. Although searches and raids were carried out, and tracking dogs were used in the area where Candela is believed to have disappeared, no concrete evidence was found that would allow the case to move forward. Additionally, the security cameras in San Vicente, which could have provided key clues, were not reviewed in time, losing valuable information. Pablo has also pointed out that, although the trafficking hypothesis was always present, it was not investigated enough in that direction. My daughter disappeared in San Vicente, 50 kilometers from the border, in a strategic location where it's easy to cross into another country, he explained. He also mentioned that he received a text message sent from Candela's phone the day after her disappearance, but assured that the writing style did not match his daughter's. He stated that it was proven that someone took her phone and wrote that. The fight of a father In these seven years, Pablo Correa De Melo has traveled to different places, both in Argentina and in Brazil, distributing flyers with Candela's photo and searching for information that may lead to her whereabouts. I have always kept searching for my daughter like on the first day, he said emotionally. For me, the issue of human trafficking still lingers, but I feel that it wasn't investigated enough. Candela's father has also requested that the case be reclassified as human trafficking or forced disappearance, since it is currently labeled as unlawful deprivation of liberty. If they believe she left on her own free will, let them say so. But in seven years, she would have had to have had contact with someone, he argued. In this sense, he announced that he would be attempting to contact the National Security Minister, Patricia Bullrich, to make the case echo. Pablo Correa De Melo made an appeal to society for everyone to collaborate in the search for his daughter and to take awareness of the gravity of disappearances. When a person disappears, it is essential for everyone to get involved, to share photos, to spread information. A second that one dedicates can help families like mine, he expressed. Additionally, he addressed a message to his daughter and to anyone who may know something about Candela's whereabouts, if you left, approach the nearest police station and let them know that you are safe. And if someone knows something, don't be afraid to speak up. Nothing will happen to you, but we need to know the truth. Hope remains alive Despite the time that has passed, Pablo Correa De Melo has not lost hope of finding his daughter. If she is alive, I feel that she is very far away. And if something happened to her here, it was something very well planned, because no trail was left, he reflected. But I won't rest until I know what happened to her. Meanwhile, Candela's case remains one of the most resonant in Misiones, and her family hopes that with the help of Justice and society, concrete answers will soon be obtained. We need to know where Candela is, not just for us, but for the entire community. This is no longer just a family matter, it affects everyone, he concluded. The disappearance of Candela Agustina De Melo remains a mystery, but her father's fight to find the truth is an example of unwavering love and perseverance that never ceases. Source: San Vicente Informa
